InfoQ Homepage News Uber Cuts Translation Cache Memory by up to 90% While Keeping P99 Latency below 1 MS

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read

Uber has redesigned its Go-based translation cache to reduce its initial memory footprint by more than 90% while keeping p99 cache miss latency below one millisecond. The hybrid architecture retains translation keys and frequently accessed values in memory while storing the remaining values on disk. The system serves millions of translations per second and maintains a cache hit rate above 99.9%.

The optimization addresses two problems identified through memory profiling across Uber's Go services. Garbage collection (GC) consumed more than 20% of CPU utilization in some services, with translations accounting for approximately 70% of allocated objects.

At Uber's scale, even small inefficiencies in memory management can add up.

The first optimization replaced Go's sync.Map with a conventional map[string]string protected by an RWMutex. The workload was predominantly read-heavy, with infrequent updates and no individual deletions. The previous implementation created multiple objects and pointers for each translation entry, increasing GC overhead. Moving to a value-based map reduced object allocations and improved CPU utilization by more than 30% in the affected service.

However, reducing object allocations did not solve the overall memory consumption problem. Translation datasets could contain two to three million keys, although individual services typically accessed only a small subset. Cache refreshes introduced another issue: the service built a replacement cache in the background before atomically swapping it with the existing one. Both copies therefore occupied memory simultaneously, causing some services to run out of memory during refreshes.

Uber considered external caching and generating service-specific translation subsets, but both introduced additional operational or maintenance costs. The team instead adopted a hybrid storage design that preserves the existing Get() and Put() API. All keys remain available in memory for fast lookups, while translation values are stored in disk-backed files.

Uber's hybrid translation cache (Source: Uber Blog Post)

The implementation uses 256 shards, each with its own read-write mutex, in-memory entries, and disk file. Six-byte hash-based keys reduce metadata overhead, with a fallback to the original key format to handle collisions. A time-based global least recently used (LRU) policy manages in-memory entries. During cache refreshes, the system uses access history to preload translations accessed within the previous 15 minutes, avoiding a cold cache after the swap.

In one example, a translation dataset that previously consumed approximately 800 MB in memory required around 40 MB for metadata after the redesign. With a configured limit of 50,000 in-memory entries, actual memory consumption typically ranged between 80 MB and 120 MB. In another reported workload, approximately 30,000 of more than four million entries were loaded in memory, while the cache hit rate remained above 99.9%. The p99 latency for disk-backed cache misses stayed below 100 microseconds.

Memory usage decreased from approximately 2.7 GB to 750 MB (Source: Uber Blog Post)

Uber's experience highlights the cost implications of in-memory caching at scale. The team recommends minimizing object references to reduce GC overhead and measuring how frequently cached values are accessed. When only a small proportion of cached data is actively used, a hybrid approach can retain frequently accessed values in memory while moving the rest to disk.

#9870. Welcome FLUX.3 Image Klein in Diffusers

Black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something new, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

With several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

For edits, each region says where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:

Everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:

FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

The text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

At the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:

Text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

At every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps shows how the image takes shape:

The fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are new to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:

Built something with FLUX.3? Share your LoRAs and pipelines on the Hub. We'd love to see them! 😎

#9868. Ransomware Attacks Increase Behind AI, but Payments Decline

Large language models and other AI systems allow a growing number of ransomware groups to create convincing phishing emails and identify sensitive data quickly.

Ransomware attacks are expanding amid cybercriminals' increasing use of AI tools, but at the same time, fewer organizations are paying ransoms, according to multiple reports released this month.

Globally, organizations are seeing far more ransomware incidents, while the number of attacks targeting US companies has remained fairly steady. In the third quarter of 2026, for example, ransomware groups claimed 2,766 breaches, an increase of nearly 40% over the previous quarter, according to threat data released by cybersecurity services firm Halcyon.

Threat groups adopting AI is likely a major reason for the increase in attacks. The ability of large language models (LLMs) to create convincing social-engineering messaging, find sensitive data quickly, and assist attackers has largely driven the surge in attacks in other nations, says Cynthia Kaiser, senior vice president of Halcyon's Ransomware Research Center and a former deputy assistant director at the FBI's Cyber Division.

Related:Africa Retakes Top Spot as Most Attacked Region, Led by Nigeria Surge

"We think AI is a big part of [the growth] because it has removed the language barrier for phishing," she says. "We're now seeing much more convincing phishing in Japanese, for example. Countries like Japan are treating this almost as a state of emergency."

Overall, the jump in claimed ransomware cases — up 31% from the first quarter and 39% from the second, according to Halcyon's report — has not necessarily resulted in more ransoms paid out.

Take the retail sector as an example: While 62% of attacks on companies succeeded in encrypting data — up from 48% in 2025 — less than a third (32%) of retailers actually paid to get the data back, nearly half of the 58% that paid in 2025, according to Sophos's "The State of Ransomware in Retail 2026" report.

Instead, a solid majority of retail firms (71%) recovered their data from backup, and most recovered within a week, Sophos found. Other sectors, such as local government and school districts, have seen declines in paying ransomware as well, says Chester Wisniewski, global field chief information security officer (CISO) at Sophos.

"None of them are paying the ransom," he says. "Whether there's extortion involved, whether data theft's involved, it kind of doesn't matter. They're largely not paying the ransom."

The number of ransomware groups claiming success took off in 2026, growing from 75 in the first quarter to 111 in the third, according to Halcyon data. While ransom amounts have continued to decline, the growth in the number of groups continues to pose a threat to companies, Sophos's Wisniewski says.

Related:AttackIQ Research Reveals How Iranian Cyber Groups Hand Off Network Access to Enable Destructive Attacks

"There's been five or six new names I've seen in just the last few weeks, so it doesn't seem like ransomware's going away at all," he says. "But its efficacy has been declining as far as generating actual money for the crooks."

The median ransom demand has dropped to $700,000 in 2026, from $2 million in 2024, according to Sophos data.

That hasn't stopped new ransomware groups from continuing to appear. At the end of the quarter, about a third of all claimed ransomware successes came from groups that didn’t exist six months earlier, says Duy-Phuc Pham, a malware researcher at Trellix.

"At the top, The Gentlemen grew from a few dozen victims a year ago to the most active group, ahead of Qilin," he says. "That kind of success makes them the obvious next target for law enforcement, which spent this year going after the shared services these groups depend on, from criminal VPNs to laundering services."

With attackers increasingly using AI, ransomware gangs will continue to broaden their campaigns against more industries in more regions — part of the reason that Europe has witnessed an increase in attacks, while US victims' share of incidents has remained the same or decreased, says Pham. AI allows attackers to create more convincing social-engineering messaging in a variety of languages, removing a significant historical barrier to targeting smaller populations.

Related:Chinese AI Project Scouts Spies in Taiwan Chip Industry

Because of the greater scale that AI enables attackers to hit, ransomware threat actors are able to widen their coverage, he says.

"When a tool can scan, exploit, and move through networks with little human effort, a small crew can do the work of a large one, hit far more victims, and do it faster," Pham says. "That fits what we see on the leak sites: more groups and more newcomers."

The manufacturing sector continues to be the top target of ransomware gangs, because suppliers and partners often share the same platforms, so a single compromise can expose engineering data beyond the targeted company, says Halcyon's Kaiser.

The sector will likely continue to be the top targeted group in 2027, especially as international organizations continue to account for a greater share in the coming year, she says.

"I'd expect continued growth, especially outside the US," Kaiser says. "The big open question is whether more attacks means more money ... countries newly feeling the pain are paying much more attention, which should improve international cooperation."

Rob is an award-winning, veteran technology journalist of more than 30 years, reporting on global cybersecurity issues, the latest offensive and defensive technologies, malware incidents, cyber conflict, and AI's impact on software and cybersecurity.

A former research engineer, Rob has written for more than two dozen publications, including CNET News.com, Dark Reading, MIT's Technology Review, Popular Science, and Wired News. He has received five awards for journalism, including Best Deadline Journalism (Online) in 2003 for his coverage of the Blaster worm. Rob also analyzes data on various trends using Python and R for both his reporting and his clients. Recent reports include analyses of the shortage in cybersecurity workers, annual vulnerability trends, and annual threat reports.

Rob holds degrees from Cornell University in Electrical Engineering and Computer Science (double major).

InfoQ Homepage News Meta TLX, a Native GPU Compiler Extension Supporting Advanced Hardware Capabilities

Nov 20, 2026 2 min read

Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to bridge the gap between high-level GPU programming abstractions and the low-level execution control required to fully exploit modern GPU architectures.

According to Meta engineers, modern GPU architectures offer advanced performance-optimization features, including warp specialization, asynchronous memory movement, tensor memory, and cluster-level execution, which depart from Triton's traditional programming model, which simplifies kernel development but abstracts away low-level execution structures.

For example, a modern FlashAttention kernel may dedicate one warp group to issuing TMA transfers while another executes tensor-core computation. A Blackwell GEMM kernel may coordinate multiple warp groups, TMEM allocations, and cluster resources simultaneously. In both cases, performance depends not only on the computation being performed, but also on how multiple execution agents cooperate.

Using these advanced features required "large amounts of architecture-specific orchestration code", as they were not readily available as Triton compilers abstractions. To address this challenge, Meta developed Triton Low-Level Extensions (TLX), designed to give engineers explicit control over GPU execution while preserving Triton's programming model.

TLX introduces a new Multiple Instructions, Multiple Warps (MIMW) execution model that bridges CUDA’s thread-level control and Triton’s block-level abstraction. It extends Triton across five key areas: warp-group orchestration, synchronization, memory orchestration, cluster execution, and optional layout.

Taken together, these capabilities allow TLX to occupy the space between Triton’s productivity and CUDA’s control. Developers retain the advantages of Python, autotuning, and blocked tensor programming while gaining direct access to the execution structures that increasingly determine performance on modern GPUs.

Meta has deployed TLX in production for several months across three major workloads. For GEM model training on thousands of NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs, TLX achieved 20–25% end-to-end Model FLOPs Utilization (MFU) with up to 2x forward-pass speedup. For In-Kernel Broadcast Optimization (IKBO) in recommendation inference, TLX delivered a 4x speedup on an H100 for a linear compression kernel and reduced compute-intensive net latency up to two-thirds in co-designed models. Finally, in distributed grouped GEMM for LLM pretraining, TLX improved performance, reliability, and maintainability across large GPU fleets for extended training periods.

Commenting on the announcement on LinkedIn, AI engineer Kritika Choudary observed:

When I wrote Flash Attention from scratch in Metal on my M2, the tile loads into threadgroup memory and where to put the barriers were where most of the thinking went, so it's nice to see TLX make that explicit.

On a similar note, Amirul Islam emphasized that:

Making warp-group handoffs explicit while leaving layouts optional feels like a useful boundary. The producer/consumer pipeline is visible in the source, without forcing every fused stage to start with manual layout bookkeeping.

Meta plans to further expand Triton TLX by adding support for additional NVIDIA, AMD, and custom accelerator architectures, automating warp-group orchestration through higher-level abstractions, and integrating TLX with torch.compile.

#9865. Welcome Muse Spark Open: open-weight frontier multimodal mixture-of-experts model from Meta

Muse Spark Open is an open-weight model from Meta. The mixture of experts model brings text, images, audio, and video into a model with approximately 816 billion parameters, around 42 billion active per token, and a context window of up to one million tokens. It generates text, giving developers a common interface for asking questions about different kinds of input.

Following Muse Glimmer, Muse Spark Open introduces a mixture-of-experts architecture at a much larger scale, and the most capable US open-weights model to date.

Meta trained Muse Spark Open for agentic coding: reading a codebase, writing and debugging code, and calling tools. It also takes images, audio, and video as input, so the same model can read a screenshot, listen to a voice note, or watch a screen recording while it works on your code. This post shows you how to run it, how to fine-tune it, and what we built with it. Find all the models here.

Meta describes Muse Spark Open as a coding-optimized model trained on real developer workflows such as multi-file refactors and long debugging sessions. Muse Spark Open is an agentic focused model that plans, acts, observes, and self-corrects over long tasks, including browsing the web with images.

The checkpoint repositories are Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B and Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4.

Muse Spark Open is the full-size model of the Muse series of models. Muse Glimmer, which Meta released in August, is a small dense model from the same series, ideal for running locally. Both models use the same tokenizer and vocabulary. The chat template follows the Muse Glimmer template, with additions for the new modalities. In Muse Spark Open the input embedding and the output layer are separate matrices of about 1.66B parameters each.

The language model has 62 layers and a hidden dimension of 8192. Each layer has 128 query heads and 16 key-value heads (grouped-query attention). Each head has 64 dimensions. The attention block has an output gate and an output normalization layer. The model also applies normalization to the queries and the keys (QK-norm). Each block combines its input and its output through a learned residual gate, not through a plain sum.

Muse Glimmer uses one dense feed-forward network in each layer. Muse Spark Open replaces this dense network with a Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) block. Each MoE block has 256 experts, and a router selects 8 experts for each token. Each expert is a feed-forward network that projects from 8192 to 4096 dimensions and back to 8192, then applies its own normalization to its output. The experts hold ~97% of the total model parameters.

Only 8 experts run per token, so the model computes each token with about 42B parameters. All 256 experts stay in memory, so deployment needs the memory of an 816B-parameter model, but runs at the much faster speed of a 42B model. The BF16 checkpoint is about 1.5 TB in safetensors format. The NVFP4 checkpoint stores the parameters in 4-bit precision with negligible loss in accuracy, specifically for NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. In transformers, the BF16 checkpoint runs across 4 nodes of 8 H200 GPUs with tensor parallelism (TP=32) and the NVFP4 runs on a single B200 node. If you want to deploy Muse Spark Open, check out the llama.cpp, vLLM, and SGLang recipes below.

A perception encoder converts images and video frames into tokens for the language model, just like Muse Glimmer. The encoder has 1.8B parameters, 50 layers, a hidden dimension of 1536, and 16 attention heads. It splits each image into 14×14 patches and produces features with 4096 dimensions. Position information comes from learned absolute embeddings and 2D RoPE. The feed-forward network in each layer uses LayerNorm and GELU. Every fourth layer and the last layer use full attention, and the other layers use sparse attention.

Muse Glimmer 30B uses an encoder with the same architecture. The design follows the Perception Encoder work from Meta. Video input goes through the same encoder as images.

Muse Spark Open accepts audio as input through its audio encoder. An audio tokenizer converts the audio into tokens, and the chat template marks the audio position with <|audio|> tokens. The encoder emits one audio token every 80 ms, which yields 12.5 tokens per second. So let’s say, you have an audio of 10 seconds, the number of input audio tokens would be 125. The encoder itself is a convolutional pyramid where each stage consists of a patch embedder of different patch sizes and 2 convolutional blocks of 1d kernels of size 7 with stride of 1. These stages are repeated for patch sizes of [16, 6, 5, 4]. At the end of the final stage, the temporal frames are fed to a final block of RMSNorm → linear projection → RMSNorm.

The context window is 1M tokens at inference. The configuration sets max_position_embeddings to 1,048,576. This includes image, video, and audio tokens in the same window as text.

Grouped-query attention keeps the KV cache small for a model of this size. Each token adds 2 × 16 heads × 64 dimensions × 62 layers = 126,976 values to the cache. In BF16, this is about 250 KB per token and about 266 GB for a full 1M-token context.

The Muse Spark Open implementation provides MuseSparkForConditionalGeneration for text generation from multimodal inputs and MuseSparkProcessor for preparing conversations. The processor combines the tokenizer, image and video processors, audio feature extractor, and chat template.

Use a DistributedConfig to configure the parallelism settings. tp_size is the number of devices across which the dense layers are sharded, and ep_size is the number of devices across which the experts are distributed.

You can initialize the model and processor as follows.

Prepare the conversation, then pass the messages to processor.apply_chat_template, enabling add_generation_prompt=True, tokenize=True, return_dict=True, and return_tensors="pt". Pass the processor output to model.generate and decode the newly generated tokens, excluding the input prefix. The processor has a lever for the reasoning effort, mapping symbolic levels (low/medium/high/xhigh) to the integers the model itself accepts (16, 64, 256, 512). Note that turning off reasoning is not possible with Muse Spark Open, so keep the model reasoning at “low” if you want to consume less tokens to solve an easier task. You can also set a numeric effort by including a line like Reasoning strength: 1 in the system prompt.

The Muse Spark Open processor expands each image marker into the number of patch tokens required by the processed image, surrounded by image boundary tokens. This expansion keeps the text positions aligned with the visual features passed to the model. The processor also handles multiple images within a single prompt.

Video prompts include frame timing as well as visual content. The processor handles videos with audios in them (which is an upgrade from Muse Glimmer thanks to the audio encoder). The processor downsamples video frames and audio to align frames together. By default, videos are sampled to 2 FPS, capped at 96 frames. You can modify this by setting the fps of the video processor:

As a general rule of thumb, videos are frames in temporal sequence, and the more you downsample, the more you will lose frames in between specific events, so you need to keep fps high if you want more accurate generations. However, there’s a trade-off because you will require more memory and increase latency for prefill. The frames are interleaved with text input that states timestamps (e.g. “Time: 3.5s”). To enable passing in videos with audio, pass load_audio_from_video=True to apply_chat_template.

Preserve the video's metadata when preparing inputs with return_metadata=True so the processor can assign the correct framerate.

The Muse Spark Open audio tower consumes a raw waveform. The processor expects mono audio at 24 kHz and pads the waveform to a multiple of 1,920 samples, corresponding to one audio embedding per 80 milliseconds. Audio supplied directly to the processor at another sample rate must first be resampled. You can do this by using the load_audio util of transformers. load_audio uses torchcodec, librosa or torchaudio backends, so make sure to have one of these installed locally before running inference.

If you want to simply use apply_chat_template with messages though, this is all handled for you under the hood:

The processor inserts the matching number of audio tokens between audio boundary markers. It also returns a mask identifying real samples, allowing the model to exclude padded audio embeddings.

Muse Spark Open uses a channel-based chat template (Harmony, first introduced by gpt-oss). Note that you don’t have to know about the internals, but it’s useful to check the channels the model routes to, in case you get low quality outputs. In the input message below:

The Muse Spark Open integration for SGLang supports text, image, audio, and video inputs. The NVFP4 reference configuration runs across four GB300 GPUs.

This configuration sets a 128K-token serving context. The plugin supplies the model implementation, checkpoint loader, and reasoning and tool-call parsers.

Muse Spark Open is available in oMLX and mlx-lm today. oQ quants optimized for oMLX are available in 3-bit and 4-bit, ready to use right away.

We tested the oQ3e quant on an M3 Ultra (512 GB). The model takes about 344 GB, leaving room for the KV cache, and runs at about 225 tok/s prefill and 21 tok/s generation with a 1024-token prompt and 128 generated tokens.

Once you download the model through the oMLX interface, you can chat with it in the built-in chat UI. From the chat UI you can add images and adjust the reasoning effort on the fly, from low to xhigh. The model’s reasoning shows up as a collapsible thinking block, separate from the final answer.

Note that it's not possible to turn reasoning off, and the default (Auto) uses xhigh. Set it to “low” if you want to use fewer tokens on easier tasks.

The language model is also available in this PR of the official mlx-lm repository. You can run it on the same high-quality oQ3e quant like this:

This is a big model, even the 3-bit quantization requires more than 256 GB of RAM, as explained above. You can also run distributed inference across multiple computers, please refer to the documentation for details.

You can deploy Muse Spark Open on Inference Endpoints with a pre-validated SGLang recipe for the NVFP4 variant which runs on either 8 × NVIDIA RTX Pro 6000 98 GB with 131072 context length, or with 8 x NVIDIA H200 141GB if you want 1048576 context length instead.

To deploy, run one command with the Hugging Face CLI:

Or open endpoints.huggingface.co/new/meta-models/Muse-Spark-Open-816B-A42B-NVFP4 and select Create Endpoint.

The endpoint exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with both Chat Completions API at /v1/chat/completions and Responses API at /v1/responses.

Any OpenAI-compatible client works with the same URL and your Hugging Face token as the API key.

You can fine-tune the 816B checkpoint with the TRL SFTTrainer. This section shows how we fine-tuned it with TRL on 8 nodes of 8 H100 GPUs. The recipe trains LoRA adapters on the attention layers. The experts stay frozen. The full script is in the TRL examples.

First, we need to split the model across 64 GPU devices. Given the large size of the model, we need to parallelize it across multiple axes. We shard the model with FSDP and split the experts across GPUs, using DistributedConfig, which tells transformers how to split the model when it loads:

In the snippet above, fsdp_size=64 shards the model across all 64 GPUs with FSDP2, and ep_size=8 splits the 256 experts of each layer into 8 groups. Transformers sends each token to the GPU that holds its expert, so each GPU trains on its own slice of the batch.

Now, we can configure the SFTConfig for our training run. We’ve performed a simple task here to adapt the model’s chat template on an open source dataset, but you could apply it to your own use case.

The core parts here are packing=True which joins examples into 2048-token sequences without padding. A block-diagonal mask keeps the examples separate. save_only_model=True saves the adapter and no optimizer state, because the trainer cannot resume a model that was sharded at load time. LoraConfig targets the four attention projections and the 256 experts of each layer stay frozen.

Then we can run this command across each node:

We trained for 500 steps, which took about 2 hours on 64 H100s, at about 8,000 tokens per second. Mean token accuracy rose from 72% to 84% and the loss fell from 1.26 to 0.57, which signals a good fine-tuning run.

Muse Spark Open is a coding and agentic model. We wanted to see that for ourselves, so we tried a mixture of multi-modal and agentic tasks that use the model's image and audio inputs. Everything below is something you can run or fork.

We combined 2-bit quantized Muse Spark open (served on llama.cpp) with the Pi coding agent to generate and iteratively improve 3D assets in Three.js. You can find the prompt here, as the model is quantized it requires a bit more steering. We get 18 TPS on llama.cpp on Mac Ultra.

We initially describe the asset, and Pi uses the model to generate Three.js code for the asset, renders the result in a browser, and captures screenshots from multiple angles. It then sends those images back to the same model on llama server for visual feedback. Pi uses that feedback to edit the code and repeats the process.

We tested Spark on computer use tasks and were amazed by the performance, so we have built a lean demo that also serves to teach you how a computer use agent works. You can also further customize this for your needs. This is both an educational example and something you can run in a few lines. You can find it here.

Muse Spark NVFP4 Browser Agent with OpenEnv and HF Sandboxes

Hugging Face Sandboxes are sandboxes built on Hugging Face Jobs for easy code execution. The demo consists of three components:

where the remote sandbox contains the environment and the browser as illustrated below.

You can easily try this with a few steps, described in the example. Start Inference Endpoint with Muse Spark Open (NVFP4 works well too!), add your endpoint URL as environmental variable, publish your OpenEnv server in Spaces and also provide that, then you can run the agent loop. Muse Spark Open sees the previous actions, system prompt, url and the screenshot of the browser to take an action, and nothing else (no DOM, no HTML code, nothing) so it’s a truly multimodal browser demo.

Finally, we wanted to push Spark’s agentic multimodality to the limits, so we set up this space that combines the model’s audio, image, and agentic properties into a browser agent. We give the model a general description of a thing we need and it interacts with the integrated browser to find options on Amazon.

Muse Spark Open takes the voice input and reasons over the type of product that meets the descriptions, searches for it on Amazon, and selects the most appropriate based on criteria.

Muse Spark Open is a full-size open-weight model from the Muse series. Start with the BF16 or NVFP4 checkpoint, or try one of the great llama.cpp quants. If you build something with Muse Spark Open, share it, and tell us in the repository’s discussions.

#9863. Apertus 1.5 Release Notes

Our latest release, Apertus 1.5, extends the 8B and 70B Apertus 1.0 models with image/audio understanding, an optional thinking mode, a four times longer context window, improved instruction-following, and better tool use. The updated 8B and 70B model weights were released to Hugging Face on July 24, 2026 under an Apache 2.0 license. Further details are now available from the project Technical Report, and summarized here.

Apertus 1.5 is a continued pretraining of the first generation model: adding 4 trillion tokens of text and multimodal training data to the 8B model and 2 trillion tokens to the 70B model, for a total of 19T and 17T, respectively. As with every Apertus release, the models are fully open: open weights, open data, open values, and full training details.

We introduce multimodality in v1.5 models in an early-fusion manner, where images and audio enter Apertus as discrete tokens in the same sequence with text tokens, instead of using a separate vision encoder. Images are tokenized with the Emu3.5 tokenizer (a 512×512 image becomes 1,024 tokens) and audio with WavTokenizer (40 tokens per second). We only extend the vocabulary, so the architecture stays unchanged and training runs at text-only speed. The models understand images and audio but generate only text.

Starting from Apertus 1.0, we continue pretraining in four stages:

Overall, more than half of the training tokens are text-only, which preserves the language abilities of Apertus 1.0. The text data is refreshed with sources such as FineWeb2-HQ+, FinePDFs, and Nemotron-CC. All new data, multimodal included, meets the same bar as before: publicly available, permissively licensed, and with robots.txt opt-outs respected retroactively. Every source is listed in apertus-data-transparency.

Post-training runs in five stages: SFT → long-context SFT → RL → DPO → charter alignment (SDPO).

Alongside the extended model capabilities, we also significantly expanded the scope of evaluations. Beyond the existing text-based evaluations used for Apertus 1.0, we added multimodal evaluations (image & audio), and thinking-mode evaluations.

The multimodal evaluations are done through MLLM-eval-suite pipeline, merging two major multimodal evaluation frameworks lmms-eval and VLMEvalKit. We also added a series of text-based benchmarks, as well as extended benchmarking for translation and multilingual capabilities, safety, and tool use. These can be found in our post-training evaluation repository, based on lm-evaluation-harness fork.

While still trailing frontier open-weight models, the new release has also significantly improved performance in coding and instruction following capabilities with Apertus 1.5 8B outperforming similarly sized open-weight models on IF and multilingual tasks. Thinking further improves performance on challenging reasoning-heavy benchmarks like AIME. The multimodal performance of the model is closer to Gemma 4 12B and other current open-weight models. Apertus 1.5 multimodal performance is competitive in spatial understanding among open-weight models and document/chart understanding among open-source models.

We also thank our collaborators and external evaluators for their help with efficient benchmarking of Apertus capabilities. In particular, Apertus 1.5 shows strong performance on Swiss Legal tasks, being on par with leading open-weight models (blog, code). Additionally, on Last Translation Benchmark, Apertus 1.5 8B presents machine translation capabilities which match GPT-OSS-20B and outperform models like Claude Haiku 4.5 or Google Translate (leaderboard, paper).

Apertus collaborates with the EvalEval Coalition to ensure fully transparent and reproducible benchmarking. We publish the Apertus 1.5 results in the Every Eval Ever (EEE) schema, a shared format that records not only scores, but also who ran the evaluation, how the model was accessed, the generation settings, and how each metric should be interpreted: details that are routinely missing from leaderboards and that often explain why similar-looking scores differ.

The results are shown in the Eval Card below, which combines the run data with benchmark and model metadata into one interpretable record, and are also available through Hugging Face Community Evals. This is the same infrastructure the UK AI Security Institute uses to publish its evaluations openly. Since our text evaluations run on our public fork of lm-evaluation-harness, which EEE supports with a dedicated converter, anyone can rerun them and compare their numbers against ours under identical settings.

Structured evaluation reporting also matters beyond research. EvalEval has mapped Evaluation Cards to AI governance requirements, including Article 55 of the EU AI Act and the GPAI Code of Practice, and found that the EEE schema can represent 56 of the 60 evaluation-reporting elements these frameworks call for. This fits how we already release Apertus: alongside the models, we publish a Public Summary of Training Content and, voluntarily, a Code of Practice document. Machine-readable evaluation records are a natural next step: making it easier for regulators, deployers, and researchers to find, interpret, and compare the evidence behind a model.

We are committed to promoting reproducible and transparent evaluation through Eval Cards and the EEE schema, and encourage other model developers to report their results in the same way, so that scores can be compared across models and organizations.

All recipes, ablations, and data mixtures are documented in the Technical Report. We aim to popularize open model development by making the v1.5 training process public and accessible. Intermediate checkpoints are hosted in our Apertus 1.5 Hugging Face collection, including the base weights, SFT, RLVR and DPO, as well as our curated training data mixes/custom datasets in Apertus 1.5 datasets collection. Sharing them allows researchers to investigate how each stage changes the model behavior.

The report covers numerous ablations on the effect of post-training data in different stages, where we observed that the multimodal data mixed in together with text data during SFT helps improve across all modalities. We also find that the benefits of multimodal reasoning traces survive the subsequent text-only reinforcement learning: starting from an SFT checkpoint trained with multimodal traces, RL improves mathematics more than when starting from a text-only checkpoint, and the advantage on reasoning tasks persists throughout training.

Proton Lumo and Infomaniak Euria are two widely used apps that have recently integrated Apertus 1.5. These deployments are linked in the Community Showcase among others - see this discussion thread for a preview.

Access to Apertus 1.5 in the form of an API for developers has been announced by a range of providers, including Swisscom, Infomaniak, Phoeniqs, and other companies listed in our General Availability guide. The report also provides details on how we work with external evaluators to test and prepare the models.

Technical instructions for running the models are in the model cards of the Apertus releases on Hugging Face and in our Quickstart guide.

Thank you for reading this blog post and being part of our community! We just celebrated five million downloads in our Hugging Face analytics 🤗 and are not slowing down. At the recent AI+X Summit in Zurich, our team announced the roadmap for Apertus 2.0: sparse/MoE architecture, ~600B total parameters, extended training schedule, with agents, mathematics and coding as priorities.

In summary: we invite you to read our report, download the models, explore the intermediate checkpoints, finetune the weights, and reproduce our evaluations. Questions that are not already covered in our publications or website FAQ are always welcome, and we would also love to hear which topics would be most useful to the community for future deep dives.

If you build with or use Apertus, please fill out the Showcase form, and reach out through the options on our Contact page. We are looking forward to highlighting more work, learning what you are building, and hearing how Apertus can be improved!

Project Apertus, et al. “Apertus 1.5: From Open Text Models to Open Multimodal Reasoners.” arXiv:2610.15542. Preprint, arXiv, October 11, 2026. https://doi.org/10.48550/arXiv.2610.15542.

#9862. [$] Added indirection allows for larger BPF programs

The BPF verifier has historically worked by tracing every possible path of execution through a program, checking, at each instruction, that various safety properties hold. This works, but it can result in an exponential increase in the number of states that need checking in programs with complicated control-flow. Alexei Starovoitov, one of the kernel's core BPF maintainers, has shared a patch set that substantially reworks how the verifier tracks states, in order to reduce the size of that exponential explosion.

InfoQ Homepage News How Google Traced GKE API Timeouts to a Linux Kernel TCP Bug

Nov 21, 2026 3 min read

Google recently detailed how three interacting bugs across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, and the Linux kernel caused intermittent Kubernetes API connectivity failures, blocking around 800 developers from deploying to production.

In January, a customer running multiple GKE clusters with Private Service Connect (PSC) for private control-plane access experienced intermittent timeouts when pods attempted to reach the Kubernetes API server.

Packet captures revealed that the control plane was responding to new TCP connection requests with stale ACK packets belonging to previously closed connections. The root cause involved three separate bugs across different networking layers. Akash Thakur, senior technical solutions engineer at Google Cloud, describes how engineers across multiple Google teams identified three root causes and ultimately addressed them:

In a race to fix the problem, we involved engineers across Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE), Private Service Connect, networking, hostnet, kernel, and the Linux upstream community, who together tracked down not one but three distinct root causes. And the final fix landed not as a config change or a feature flag, but as a patch to the Linux kernel itself.

The investigation identified three interacting causes: packet reordering in PSC, Envoy's half-close behavior preventing TCP connections from being properly closed, and a Linux kernel bug that discarded certain reordered FIN packets.

Thakur describes a complex troubleshooting case involving I/O timeouts across Private Service Connect, virtual network interfaces, and the Linux TCP state machine, which ultimately revealed a kernel issue leaving sockets stuck indefinitely in the FIN_WAIT_2 state. Thakur explains:

Most networking cases resolve at one layer. You find the misconfigured firewall rule, the exhausted connection pool, the miscalculated MTU. You fix it and move on. This one was different because the symptom — i/o timeout on a connection that never completed — was the same whether you were looking at the Private Service Connect layer, the kernel's TCP state machine, or Envoy's connection management. Every layer had a plausible explanation, and every explanation was incomplete.

The issue was addressed through three coordinated fixes over several weeks: Google first rolled back a Private Service Connect change to restore connectivity, then corrected the proxy protocol handling and added regression tests. Finally, a Linux kernel patch, authored by Eric Dumazet, formerly a software engineer at Google, fixed the underlying TCP issue. Rohan Karne, managing director at Google Cloud, comments:

This is the unglamorous reality of mission-critical platform engineering—methodically ruling out the obvious suspects and digging into packet captures until you find the kernel root cause.

Thakur highlights how individually reasonable behaviors across networking, proxies and operating systems can combine into complex infrastructure failures. Packet captures at multiple network layers were essential to identifying the problem, while correlating network symptoms with infrastructure changes helped establish the connection between the three bugs. Guangba Yu, a postdoctoral researcher at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, highlights:

For AIOps and chaos engineering, the transferable method is organizing simultaneous path observations, protocol state, and rollout events while distinguishing symptom recovery from state-machine correction. This anonymized case supplies no population failure rate and does not explain all API timeouts.

Justin Garrison, field CTO at Sidero, notes:

At first I was excited to read this article that leads to a kernel patch which are always fun. It turns out GKE just runs a kernel from 3 years ago (6.1) and the bug was already fixed upstream and they had to backport it.

The kernel fix was merged into Linux 6.9.7 and backported to the 6.6 and 6.1 LTS branches, reaching GKE customers in version 1.33.5 and later.

#9859. Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

One of the oldest running bug disclosure programs announced it would shorten public disclosure timelines to vendors from 120 days to 30 over the next 14 months.

Google will soon drastically reduce the disclosure deadlines of vulnerabilities prior to publicly disclosing them, and the move has sparked concern among some cybersecurity professionals.

Project Zero, Google's third-party vulnerability remediation program, currently follows what it describes as "90+30" policy: 90 days to remediate a vulnerability and an extra 30-day "soak time" to allow for patch rollout before publicly disclosing the bug. This will no longer be the case. As of the announcement on Nov. 13, Google changed its policy to disclose 90 days after reporting to the vendor. As of Feb. 2, 2027, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 60 days. As of Jan. 3, 2028, vulnerabilities will be disclosed after 30 days.

In a blog post outlining the decision, Google's Natalie Silvanovich wrote that while the intention of 90+30 was to encourage faster patching while giving vendors time to deliver patches, "The advent of AI-assisted vulnerability discovery and exploitation has changed the threat landscape such that the vulnerability remediation timeline encouraged by our disclosure policy is clearly insufficient."

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Specifically, Silvanovich noted that large language models have enabled threat actors to find and exploit vulnerabilities much faster in today's AI era.

"A vulnerability reported today presents a much higher immediate risk to users than one reported last year. In this new environment, it is crucial that vendors move towards remediating vulnerabilities faster," she wrote. "LLMs have also decreased the time it takes for attackers to reverse engineer and exploit a vulnerability based on a patch, to the extent that zero patch-to-exploitation time is a reasonable, though imperfect, model of attacker behavior."

Project Zero is not a conventional bug disclosure program. Founded in 2014, the organization was established specifically so Google could help facilitate the safe reporting and disclosure of high-severity, high-impact vulnerabilities found in widely used software and hardware. That said, Project Zero's move reflects a broad inundation of AI-discovered vulnerabilities, and where Google goes, the rest of the industry may follow.

As for whether such a thing is good, bad, or necessary for the cybersecurity industry, experts appear to be split.

Disclosure timelines are a key part of the vulnerability ecosystem. When a researcher or firm discovers a vulnerability and submits it to the software developer responsible, a standard timeline is usually designated for the developer to fix the vulnerability; such deadlines are usually 90 or 120 days, but it varies depending on the bug, disclosure policy, and circumstances.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

If the software developer ignores the bug report, is slow to address it, or declines to communicate with the researcher, the researcher may choose to disclose the flaw at the end of the disclosure timeline to inform security teams and practitioners of the looming threat. These timelines hold software vendors accountable and encourage them to maintain secure software, but it's not perfect science.

Oftentimes, the researcher and software developer will work together to coordinate a disclosure date so relevant research, patches, and mitigations are ready at the same time. Sometimes, if the bug is especially dangerous or requires more time to fix, the timeline may change and the technical details and proof-of-concept exploits will be held until a later date.

It's worth noting there are no standard requirements between platforms. HackerOne keeps its default disclosure timeline to 30 days, though it's broadly set at the program level by each vendor customer, and many HackerOne programs set longer timelines. Bugcrowd researchers and vendors generally coordinate timelines; program rules again supersede standards.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

TrendAI's Zero Day Initiative (which is not a platform but a vendor-agnostic vulnerability disclosure program) uses a standard disclosure timeline of 120 days for responsive vendors that release working patches, and shorter timelines for vulnerabilities that result from faulty patches.

It remains to be seen whether the larger industry will follow Project Zero's lead. Dustin Childs, ZDI's head of threat awareness, calls Google's decision "a bold move to be sure, especially considering the explosion of bug reports coming in thanks to AI assisted discovery."

However, he worries about how shorter timelines may impact remediation quality. "I fear it will lead to patches that don’t fully address the vulnerability. We see that happen at 120 days," Childs says. "We’ll be watching closely to see how this change impacts vendors and researchers alike."

Alex Rice, cofounder, CISO, and CTO at HackerOne, tells Dark Reading that he expects the industry to move in Google's direction, though not necessarily in lockstep. He argues that patch soak time no longer protects defenders, given how quickly attackers can exploit flaws now. And because Project Zero is a disclosure program for vulnerabilities with demonstrated impact and not a bug bounty platform that addresses a broad range of flaws, Google is in a unique position to set aggressive expectations.

"The specifics will still vary by program, severity, and whether a fix is realistic, and platforms like ours will need to support that flexibility," Rice says. "But the direction isn’t in question. Organizations should plan for 30 days as the baseline expectation that will shrink even further."

Between stories from this year about AI models capable of discovering zero-day bugs off of human language prompts and vulnerability coordinators fighting huge spikes in bug reporting volumes the past couple of years, Google's position seems defensible. The tech giant isn't alone in its move either: In January, Anthropic's own coordinated disclosure policy will shorten from 90 days to 30 days for high- and critical-severity bugs, and 45 days for all other cases.

But not everyone agrees. Expel principal threat researcher Marcus Hutchins took issue with the move in a post to X, where he noted that 2026 has already seen far more CVEs than 2025. "Sure, there are some vendors who just sit on bugs forever and don't make any effort to patch them. But there's way more overworked & underpaid teams, non-profits, and solo projects who are patching bugs as fast as they physically can," he wrote.

Katie Moussouris, CEO of Luta Security and a pioneer in vulnerability disclosure, largely agrees. As she tells Dark Reading, even AI firms currently struggle to patch the issues they find, leaving volunteers and less resourced firms even further back against the wall. "A deadline doesn't magically manifest a fix."

"Researchers and AI companies are burying maintainers in bug reports and not doing enough to help fix them. This isn't even a matter of model access or token cost. The AI companies themselves can't even close the gap," she says. "Anthropic reports that 629 of the 5,087 vulnerabilities it disclosed have been patched. OpenAI's Patch the Planet initiative, run with security engineers from Trail of Bits, has written patches for a third of the 2,055 issues it found, and 23% have been accepted upstream."

[Editor's Note: After publication, a Trail of Bits spokesperson told Dark Reading that of the most recent finding of 2,162 issues found, 733 have a patch written, and among those, 506 (or about 69%) have been accepted or merged upstream.]

A Google spokesperson tells Dark Reading that in creating the new policy, the company solicited feedback from the vendors Project Zero reports the most vulnerabilities to, including open source projects.

"The general consensus was that these timelines are achievable, and most open source projects are almost there," the spokesperson says. "Every vulnerability that Project Zero reported against a volunteer-maintained project in 2026 was fixed in 30 days, except for one, which was fixed in 31 days. Open source projects are among the vendors who will need to make the fewest changes to meet our new policy, as they are already doing so well."

While one side of the argument disagrees with the rollout of shorter timelines, the other side sees it as inevitable or necessary to respond to how attackers now use AI to pursue their goals. HackerOne's Rice says that right now, teams are not ready to deal with a 30-day turnaround, but Google's move may offer an opportunity at the boardroom level to convince technology and executive partners that remediation is a shared responsibility.

"If you're a security team struggling to keep up, don't waste time playing the victim. Take this as a gift," he says. "Ask for dedicated engineering capacity for security fixes, pre-agreed remediation SLAs, automated validation and retesting, and the authority to ship mitigations while the full fix is built. The teams that turn this pressure into that conversation will be far ahead of the ones hoping for external relief."

Casey Ellis, founder of Bugcrowd and The disclose.io Project, says this is a necessary evolution, even if it feels aggressive. In the wake of proliferated vulnerability discovery, the timeline shortening "puts productive pressure on response and fix pipelines."

Ellis says he feels the typical targets of Project Zero researchers are in "decent shape," but community norms tend to follow Google's lead on CVE timelines, so the move could carry larger impact.

"My main concern would be companies that maintain safety-critical systems or those that are otherwise logistically difficult to update; a security fix doesn't always end with a patch, and more often than not, it doesn't," he says. "The Project Zero changes will ultimately reveal (and hopefully shrink or close) the readiness gap for many PSIRT teams, products, and hosted service providers, but unless product vendors become proactive about this aspect of vulnerability discovery and disclosure it is likely to be a bumpy ride for some."

This story was updated on Nov. 18, 2026 at 8:47 a.m. ET, with additional context shared by a Trail of Bits spokesperson regarding figures included in the article.
