#9835. Six Password Reset Vulnerabilities and How to Prevent Them

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

Autonomous security testing powered by AI agents. Powerful. Accurate. Actionable. hackerme.ai

This is an example, not a report from a customer. Imagine a support inbox: someone never asked for a password reset, but they received a "your password was changed" email, and now their login no longer works. Their old password was long and unique. Nobody guessed it.

Nobody needed to. A reset flow is a way into an account without the current password, by design. A valid reset link may let whoever holds it set a new password. Whether that is enough to take the account depends on other controls: a second factor at the reset step, a prompt to re-authenticate, a notification the real owner sees in time, session invalidation after the change, or a token that has already expired or been used.

OWASP calls this functionality "a common source of vulnerabilities" even though it "looks straightforward and easy to implement" (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet). The usual weak points sit at six places in the flow. Run the active tests only on systems you own or have written permission to test.

When someone types an address into "Forgot password", the response should not reveal whether an account exists. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet lists "We just sent you a password reset link" and "This email address doesn't exist in our database" as incorrect responses, and gives the correct one: "If that email address is in our database, we will send you an email to reset your password" (OWASP Authentication Cheat Sheet).

The message is the easy part. The Forgot Password Cheat Sheet also asks for responses that "return in a consistent amount of time," for example by sending the email asynchronously instead of exiting early for unknown addresses. A page that answers in a few milliseconds for unknown addresses and noticeably later for real ones tells an attacker the same thing as a different message.

Then rate-limit the endpoint. OWASP recommends per-account rate limiting or a CAPTCHA, because otherwise an attacker can flood a user's inbox. Return the same 429 Too Many Requests whether or not the account exists (RFC 6585, section 4), or the limiter itself becomes an enumeration oracle. Do not lock the account: OWASP notes that a forgotten-password attack should not produce a lockout, because that lets anyone deny access to users whose names they know.

Many frameworks make it easy to build an absolute URL from "the current host". In a reset email, that convenience is the vulnerability. PortSwigger describes password reset poisoning: an attacker submits a reset request for the victim with a Host header pointing at a domain they control, the site sends a genuine token, and the link inside points at the attacker. If the victim clicks it, or a mail scanner fetches it, the token is delivered to the attacker (PortSwigger: Password reset poisoning).

OWASP's instruction is direct: "Don't rely on the Host header while creating the reset URLs." Use one configured HTTPS base URL per environment, and reject host names you do not serve. Treat X-Forwarded-Host the same way: trust it only from your own proxy.

OWASP lists the properties every reset token needs: generated with a cryptographically secure random number generator, long enough to resist brute force, linked to an individual user, invalidated after use, stored securely, and expiring after an appropriate period.

Here is a minimal sketch in Python that follows those properties. It is something to adapt, not a drop-in library.

secrets.token_urlsafe(32) uses Python's module for security tokens, which documents 32 bytes (256 bits) of randomness as sufficient for the typical case (Python docs: secrets). Never use random, timestamps, user IDs or sequential values. Store only a hash, so a leaked database does not contain working links. For a long random token, a fast hash such as SHA-256 is a reasonable choice; slow password hashing is meant for secrets people choose (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet). Issuing a new token should burn older ones for that user. An expired, used or unknown token should produce the same generic error page.

The sketch is single-process and in-memory. In a real application, two requests can redeem the same token at once, so marking it used must be one atomic database operation that succeeds only if it changes exactly one unused, unexpired row.

The token sits in a URL, and URLs travel.

OWASP asks reset pages to send Referrer-Policy: no-referrer. When no policy is set, browsers default to strict-origin-when-cross-origin, which sends only the origin on cross-origin requests (MDN: Referrer-Policy). A missing header is not proof that the token leaks to third parties in current browsers. It is a missing layer: the default still sends the full URL on same-origin requests, and a looser policy elsewhere on the site would apply.

Analytics, chat widgets and session-replay tools on the reset page can read location.href. The cleanest pattern is a reset page with no third-party scripts. Mail scanners can also open the link before the user does. If a GET burns the single-use token, the real user may find it "already used". Show the form on GET, and consume the token only on POST.

If an attacker already had a session, a new password alone does not remove them. OWASP recommends invalidating existing sessions, or asking the user whether to do so, and advises against signing the user in automatically after the reset. The Session Management Cheat Sheet lists a completed password change among the events that should require reauthentication (OWASP Session Management Cheat Sheet).

Send a notification that the password was changed, without the password in it, as OWASP recommends. In the example above, that email is what turned a silent change into a support ticket. Include a way to report "this wasn't me" that does not depend on the account's current password.

Use two test accounts you control, and staging where possible. We have not run the commands below against a live site.

Submit the form for a real test address and for an address that does not exist, and compare status, visible message, size and timing. You want the same status and message for both. A "no such user" error is a leak. Small size differences can come from a CSRF token; timing needs many requests before it means anything.

In staging, send the same request with a foreign Host (and again with X-Forwarded-Host) and read the email that arrives. If the link points at the foreign host, that header is being trusted. A 404 or 421 from the proxy only shows that this request was refused; read the link-building code as well.

With a test account, reuse a spent link, use the older of two links, wait past expiry, and open the page with GET before submitting the form. The last check shows whether a GET burns the token. Look at the reset page for Referrer-Policy and third-party scripts. After a reset, a second browser that was already signed in should be signed out or asked to authenticate again.

If every step behaved as intended for these test accounts, this flow did what you asked when you tested it. Other recovery paths, and the difference between staging and production, still need their own review.

We are the HackerMe team, and we build a free scanner for public pages and headers. It cannot read reset emails or token storage.

InfoQ Homepage News Google Announces Agent Compute Engine for Secure AI Agent Execution

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read

Google recently announced Agent Compute Engine, a managed service that runs AI agents in isolated microVMs, with checkpointing capabilities to suspend and resume execution environments. The design keeps credentials, API keys, and OAuth refresh tokens outside the agent sandbox, using an external Agent Gateway to authenticate requests and inject the required secrets.

Google designed Agent Compute Engine to address three requirements at global scale: keeping sandboxes free of exploitable credentials, even when agents make mistakes; minimizing the cost and latency of resuming idle agents; and preserving persistent workspaces across sessions and operating system updates. The infrastructure team writes:

Agent Compute Engine achieves this by using copy-on-write memory sharing to run multiple agents on a single operating system template, and pausing idle microVMs via fast checkpoint and restore.

In the deep dive "Inside Agent Compute Engine," Ramanathan Venkatapathy and Rohit Jnagal, distinguished engineers at Google, describe the service’s architecture, covering microVM isolation, credential management, agent identity, storage, and scheduling at scale. They explain the strict separation between the agent harness and sandbox:

The orchestration harness (the brain) runs completely outside the execution sandbox (the hands), helping ensure that untrusted guest environments only execute explicit commands dispatched by the harness and stream output back. This boundary establishes a deterministic audit trail correlating every harness-initiated tool call with expected compute activity inside the sandbox.

The architecture supports four main workload categories: interactive consumer and enterprise agents that execute code, browse the web, and perform actions; persistent Linux workspaces for autonomous software engineering; large-scale parallel environments for model evaluation and reinforcement learning; and lightweight, sandboxed execution environments for dynamic logic in Google services.

Venkatapathy and Jnagal also describe how the cloud provider uses the platform internally for Gemini, Gemini for Business, the agentic development platform Antigravity, and model evaluation workloads.

Separately, Google offers Agent Substrate, an open-source, Kubernetes-native runtime for running AI agents in isolated environments. Agent Substrate manages sandbox lifecycles independently of the underlying compute infrastructure, allowing idle agents to be suspended while preserving their state and resuming execution on available workers when needed.

In the article "Google's Agent Compute Engine: A MicroVM Sandbox With No Credentials Inside, and What Google Has Not Shipped Yet," Harel Asaf, AI specialist at Elementor, examines the security architecture, the separation of credentials from agent execution environments, and the gaps between Google's announcement and what is currently available. Asaf warns:

The deep dive gives no boot time, price or density figure for Agent Compute Engine itself. It says developers will control each environment's image, identity, network access and lifecycle, while Google manages the fleet, and that the service is targeted for preview in the coming months. The numbers in the announcement belong to Agent Substrate.

Google is not the only provider offering managed, isolated execution environments for AI agents, with AWS and Azure providing similar capabilities through Bedrock AgentCore and Foundry Agent Service. However, Google’s approach keeps credentials outside agent sandboxes and injects them through an external gateway.

Google also expanded its agent governance capabilities with centralized identity and policy enforcement: the governance stack includes Agent Gateway for traffic control and policy enforcement, Agent Registry for tracking approved agents and tools, SPIFFE-based Agent Identity for authentication and auditing, and OpenTelemetry-compatible observability for monitoring model calls and tool invocations.

Agent Compute Engine is not yet available, and pricing has not been announced. The cloud provider is targeting a preview in the coming months. While Agent Substrate is portable across Kubernetes environments, Agent Compute Engine itself is limited to Google Cloud.

Presented by: Kiran Gangadharappa - Engineering Advisor at Harness, and Scott Davis - Senior Engineering Manager at Harness

#9832. Turning Database Grading into RL Rewards: Post-Training Agents with ThinkingBox

This is the follow up to our first blog post, The Agent Said It Was Done. The Database Disagreed. ThinkingBox-Training is now available on GitHub.

We built ThinkingBox to evaluate an agent's work by comparing the final database state with the expected outcome. We then used the same kind of executable signal as a reward on training tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench. For Qwen3.8-27B, average success rose from 51.70% to 60.78%, while tasks completed correctly on all twenty attempts rose from 38 to 107 with 50 GRPO steps.

Figure 1. ThinkingBox turns executable checks of terminal database state into rewards for post-training agents on tasks outside ThinkingBox-Bench.

We built ThinkingBox to catch agents that say they are done when they are not.

Each of its 507 tasks in ThinkingBox-Bench (our benchmark dataset) hands an agent a real backend and a set of tools, lets it work, then checks what really changed in the database. In the first post, we caught a model closing a customer's ticket as resolved while the carrier exception behind it was still open. Nine competent-looking tool calls, one wrong database row.

Then we noticed what we had built. For most tasks, an executable check can return 1 or 0 directly from the final database state. That is not just a grader. This can be a reward function.+

So we constructed a training pool from ThinkingBox-format tasks outside the benchmark and used their executable outcomes as rewards. The catch was choosing which tasks are suitable for agent training: most tasks are either already solved or hopeless for the model in front of you, and both teach it nothing.

Difficulty is policy-relative: a task is hard for the current model only until that model learns it.

We call this offline policy-relative difficulty. We estimated each task's success probability once using the base policy before training and kept the selected training pool fixed throughout the run.

We used offline policy-relative difficulty to build the training pool, then fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B with GRPO for 50 steps. To recap, we evaluate each of the 507 benchmark tasks 20 times. pass@1 measures average success across all 10,140 attempts. pass@20 measures the share of tasks solved at least once. Observed 20/20 measures the share of tasks that pass every recorded attempt.

Table 1. Qwen3.8-27B results before and after 50 steps of GRPO on the offline-selected training pool.

Training sharply increased repeatable success, with a small decline in at-least-once coverage. The rest of the post explains how we selected practice tasks, built the reward loop, and measured that tradeoff.

What does that improvement look like on one task? A traveler requests a room downgrade, but company policy requires manager approval first. Before training, the agent changed the booking and issued refunds without approval in 15 of 20 attempts. After RL fine-tuning, it preserved the booking and payment state in all 20.

Figure 2. One corporate hotel-booking task, 20 attempts per model. The base Qwen3.8-27B model changed the booking without required manager approval in 15 attempts. The RL fine-tuned model preserved booking and payment state in all 20; all expected records matched in 19.

In a hurry? The headline result is above. The implementation is in Run the training stack.

ThinkingBox-Bench grades agents on the database records they leave behind. Each of its 507 tasks starts a real backend, hands the agent a set of MCP tools and a simulated LLM user with private context, and at the end runs executable checks against the terminal database state. Checks are against the backend record that needs to be correct, not the specific tool calls. This incentivizes the model to discover possibly new solution paths rather than “rediscover” the human-backed solution, that might be suboptimal albeit correct.

In our first post we ran eighteen models through that benchmark twenty times each and reported a gap that headline accuracy hides. Kimi-K3 solved 93.89% of tasks at least once but completed only 68 of 507 tasks (13.41%) on all twenty recorded attempts. Claude Opus 5 inverted it: narrower coverage, far more consistency.

And bigger or better model did not close it. Claude Opus 5.5 scored 0.66 percentage points higher than Claude Opus 5 on pass@1, yet passed exactly the same number of tasks, 241, on all twenty attempts. That gain in headline accuracy bought zero additional dependability.

If you are choosing a model for work that touches production database records, pass@1 should not be read alone. Observed 20/20 shows which tasks succeed on every attempt, which is closer to what production reliability requires.

The executable terminal-state verdict was also the training reward. Before unpacking the training loop, here is what changed on the sealed benchmark.

After training Qwen3.8-27B, we evaluated the selected step-50 checkpoint on the 507-task benchmark it had never trained on. The 507 tasks represent an out-of-distribution test set: their domains, databases, and most MCP tools were not encountered during RL training.

Table 2. ThinkingBox-Bench pass@1 (%) by domain, for selected models from our first blog's Table 2 and our fine-tuned model for different domains and overall. Observed 20/20 numbers are over the entire benchmark with 507 tasks. Each model is evaluated on all 507 tasks for 20 repeated trials. Bold marks the column leader; underline marks the runner-up.

The headline result is the observed-20/20 row in Table 1. A 27B model that initially completed 38 (7.5%) of ThinkingBox-Bench on every attempt now completes 107 (21.1%) on every attempt, almost thrice. For comparison, observed 20/20 for Kimi-K3 is 68, GPT-5.4 with 128, GPT-6 Astra has 231, and Claude Opus 5.5 leads with 241.

Average success and repeatability produce different orderings. In Table 2, we notice that GPT-5.6 Sol scored slightly higher on pass@1 than the RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B (61.91% versus 60.78%) but passed fewer tasks on all 20 recorded attempts: 82 versus 107. Claude Sonnet 4.6 scored lower on pass@1, at 59.19%, yet passed nearly the same number of tasks every time, at 102. Neither metric alone captures the full picture.

The observed pattern is consistent with sharpening: repeatable success rose while at-least-once coverage fell slightly. This is in-line with prior work. One explanation is that probability distribution moved toward trajectories that work repeatedly while some low-probability paths disappeared.

Overall, the model did not become broader. It became more repeatable. The next question is where those gains landed.

Figure 3. Domain-level base scores, RLFT scores, and percentage-point changes. Green change cells show gains and red cells show declines; blue shading indicates the score level within each metric.

Pass@1 and observed 20/20 rose in all five domains. Pass@20 was mixed: it increased in neobank and consulting, but declined in retail, travel, and auto insurance. Auto insurance had the largest breadth loss (−7.0 points), while retail had the largest observed-20/20 gain (+24.5 points).

The first post priced consistency using simple math: divide the estimated cost of the full 20-run campaign by the number of tasks the model passed every single time.

Cost per dependable task = estimated cost of the 507 × 20 campaign ÷ tasks passing 20/20

Applying the same cost math to the fine-tuned checkpoint's measured token usage:

Table 3. Estimated evaluation cost and dependability for base and RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B. Cost per successful attempt divides total estimated campaign cost (507 x 20) by the number of passing attempts.

At $8.00 per dependable task, the fine-tuned model came close to GPT-5.4 ($6.80), GPT-6 Astra ($7.45), and Claude Opus 5.5 ($7.80) in the companion comparison.

Figure 4 prices cost per successful attempt against pass@1.

Figure 4. The golden arrow traces Qwen3.8-27B base pareto cost position to the RLFT (diamond): pass@1 rises from 51.70% to 60.78% while estimated cost per successful attempt falls from $0.177 to $0.139. Ringed circles mark the Pareto cost frontier.

The move places the fine-tuned checkpoint close to GPT-5.6 Sol, although GPT-5.6 Sol remains cheaper and slightly higher on pass@1. Four models priced in our paper fall outside the plotted range.

The dollar values are a comparative serving index, not invoice or cloud bills. Serving the fine-tuned checkpoint would be the same as the base model. The calculation includes model inference cost, and excludes training run and policy-probe cost for curating the training dataset.

These results tell us what moved. The next sections explain the training loop and why selecting the right tasks matters the most.

Figure 5. The six stages, now in context: candidate tasks feed in, the first three run once offline, the last three repeat for every group in the training run. The trained checkpoint is evaluated against ThinkingBox-Bench.

Selection runs once, offline, against the base policy model, i.e in this case Qwen3.8 27B; training then uses that fixed pool that has been curated. The dashed amber arrow in Figure 5 marks the path we did not take: re-probing difficulty during the training run.

Every rollout is a complete episode, not a text completion. It gets a fresh backend, an isolated MCP session, and GPT-5 Chat as the simulated user. Most rewards come from deterministic terminal-state checks; a minority of narrow rubric requirements can invoke the configured judge (GPT-5 Chat).

Training and evaluation must interpret Qwen output identically. That includes reasoning extraction, tool calls, argument typing, rendering, and isolated task state. Otherwise the reward measures a different agent from the one evaluated. The shared interpretation code is in trainer/core/tb_interpret.py.

For the reference run, we ran full-parameter RL fine-tuned Qwen3.8-27B on 187 tasks using token-mean GRPO. Each update generated 18 groups of 8 rollouts, or 144 episodes, across 24 H100s. Training ran synchronously with parameter and optimizer offload; AdamW used a 1e-6 learning rate and zero weight decay. We ran the training for 50 steps.

Zero-variance groups were replaced DAPO-style during training. System errors were handled separately: a backend timeout is not an incorrect agent outcome, so affected groups were refilled rather than scored as failures.

That explains how retained tasks were trained. The remaining question is which tasks entered the training pool.

Before diving deep into the selection of training tasks, a disclaimer:

No ThinkingBox-Bench task was included in the RL training pool. The benchmark was reserved for evaluation.

ThinkingBox-Bench is out-of-distribution relative to the RL training pool: its domains, databases, policies, and most tools were not encountered during RL training. The two sets still share the ThinkingBox framework, simulated-user machinery, executable terminal-state grading, a few common tools, and a similar task style. These shared elements limit the scope of the transfer claim.

Why selection matters comes down to one arithmetic fact about GRPO. If all eight rollouts fail, the reward vector is [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. If all eight succeed, it is [1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1]. In either case, centering within the group produces no task-reward advantage because no trajectory did better than another.++

A mixed group such as [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1] supplies the contrast GRPO can learn from. That distinction is expensive for a stateful agent: every rollout provisions an isolated backend, runs a real tool session, and calls a separate model to play the user.

The question that shaped this work was therefore not only which model or optimizer? It was: which candidate tasks should enter the fixed training pool?

We used an offline pass-rate filter on the posterior to select the training pool. It estimates which tasks are likely to produce contrasting terminal rewards under the base policy.

So we probe. Each candidate task is run repeatedly against the base policy model. The plain-language rule is simple: tasks the model always fails are unlikely to teach it yet; tasks it always passes are already learned; tasks it solves sometimes are where outcomes can provide contrast.

Each candidate task is run n times, producing k successes. We model its latent success probability with Jeffreys posterior probability:

success probability | k successes in n probes ~ Beta(k + ½, n − k + ½)

Figure 6. Offline policy-relative difficulty is estimated from repeated base-policy probes and used to retain tasks likely to produce contrasting rewards.

We partition the unit interval into five buckets with boundaries at 0.08, 0.40, 0.60, and 0.90, chosen as hyperparameters for these runs. Each task is assigned to the bucket containing the greatest posterior mass:

Further details are in Appendix C.4 of our ThinkingBox paper.

Figure 7. Zooming in, one task through all six stages: GPT-5.4 screening, base-model probes, difficulty classification, a rollout group, terminal-state grading, and a GRPO update.

Figure 7 follows one candidate task that can potentially enter the training pool. For the Qwen3.8 27B full-parameter pool, GPT-5.4 first served as a solvability screen. The base policy then succeeded on few of the probes e.g 3 of 8, producing a Beta(3.5, 5.5) posterior. Its largest mass, 54.0%, fell in the Difficult band.

When sampled for training, the task produced the mixed reward group [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1]. Successful trajectories therefore received above-mean task advantage and failed trajectories below-mean advantage, giving GRPO contrast to learn from. A different policy model could place the same task in a different difficulty band.

The final Qwen3.8-27B curated training pool contained 187 tasks.

Nothing about the trajectory. The reward is the task's own executable verdict.

When an episode ends, the sandbox extracts what actually changed in the backend and runs the task's deterministic checks against the terminal state. Any trajectory that produces the correct end state passes. Wrong, missing, or extra side effects fail. The reward is 1 or 0.

In the benchmark, the database grader can be thought of as the “examiner”: it caught agents that reported success and left the wrong record. In training, the same kind of check can be seen as the “teacher” on a different, disjoint set of tasks.

We release the data-selection, rollout, reward, and Verl integration used to train Qwen3.8-27B in microsoft/thinkingbox-training. The repository README is the entry point. The detailed guides are:

Tested on Linux and WSL with Python 3.12 and uv. You need NVIDIA GPUs with a compatible CUDA/NCCL stack, a local Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint, and OpenAI-compatible endpoints for the simulated user and judge. The validated reference configuration uses 3 nodes x 8 H100 GPUs; smaller custom configurations depend on model size, context length, and rollout concurrency.

The public sample task list exercises the interface. It is not the private 187-task training pool used for the reported run. Supply an authorized training source that remains disjoint from the public benchmark.

Start with the publicly provided samples, or add your own authorized dataset in ThinkingBox format. Then run the repository's preparation script:

The script aggregates policy probes, applies offline policy-relative difficulty filters and benchmark exclusions, and writes the selected train.yaml and test.yaml files. docs/data-preparation.md documents the input fields, loader contract, and complete command.

The launcher configures training; it does not provision hosts. On the reference three-node topology, export the same environment on every node, mount CHECKPOINT_DIR at the same absolute path, then start Ray:

In a separate terminal, start the OpenEnv compatibility proxy for the Qwen chat template from the ThinkingBox Training checkout. It listens on port 8014 and forwards to vLLM on 8001:

Keep it running during evaluation. From another terminal, check readiness:

Start OpenEnv as in the first post, with OPENENV_TB_CONFIG pointing to this thinkingbox.yaml and OPENENV_TB_DATASET to $THINKINGBOX_DATA. Once /ready succeeds, run the full protocol of 507 tasks × 20 attempts:

The useful part of this work is not one Qwen3.8-27B checkpoint. It is the training loop and training data curation that turns executable outcomes into rewards.

#9828. Does Your Model Run on AWS Trainium? Look It Up

In a previous post, we introduced TorchNeuron, the native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium (the torch-neuronx package). With it, Transformers runs its own modeling code on Trainium, as it does on any other device, so any Transformers model on the Hub may run. Which ones actually do?

The torch-neuronx model support Space answers that question for the most popular models on the Hub. It tells you whether a model runs unmodified on Trainium, and gives you the script to run it yourself.

The Space opens on the Selected view: our own selection of models picked among the top models on the Hub by downloads and by trending score. Each row gives the result, the number of Trainium cores the model is sharded over, the wall time of the run (compilation included) and the peak device memory.

To look up a given model, switch to the Trending or Downloads view and type part of its name. These views follow the Hub's own rankings, one task at a time, whether a model was tested or not. When a model was left out on purpose, the Space tells you why (most of the time it was not prioritized, sometimes it is truly incompatible). You can also pick the versions of the Neuron compiler (neuronx-cc) and of Transformers to look at.

At the time of writing, only Transformers models are tested, and our selection is limited to text-generation and image-text-to-text models. We plan to expand to diffusers, sentence transformers, and other transformers tasks.

Select a model to see how to run it. The Space lists the Neuron stack the model was tested on, the packages to install on top of it, and the run.py script that ran. The script follows the recipe of the TorchNeuron announcement: it loads the model with from_pretrained, sharded when it needs to be, then generates with a static cache and torch.compile(backend="neuron").

On a Trainium2 (trn2) instance with that stack, for example in the AWS Neuron Deep Learning Container, install the packages, then run:

No need for torchrun: the script launches its own torch.distributed ranks when the model is sharded.

A first run starts by compiling the model's graphs. To skip that step, copy the graphs the same compiler built during the test, from the public NEFF cache bucket. The Space gives you the command, with the right compiler version:

Each test loads the model on a trn2 instance, sharded over the smallest number of Trainium cores that can hold its weights. Most models are sharded with tensor parallelism. Mixture-of-experts models without a tensor-parallel plan use expert parallelism only. The test then generates 32 tokens and checks them. On a single core, the tokens are compared with those of a CPU run of the same checkpoint. When the model is sharded, a small judge model checks that the text is fluent English.

At the time of writing, only models that fit on 4 Trainium2 devices are tested, which means 16 cores at most. A PASS says nothing about throughput, or about longer generations.

Everything the Space shows comes from the public aws-neuron/torch-neuronx-model-support dataset, with one Parquet file per pair of neuronx-cc and library versions.

Each row holds a model's result, the error when it failed, the versions of the whole stack and the run.py that ran. You can query it directly:

The dataset card gives the exact meaning of each result.

Next time you wonder whether a model runs on Trainium, look it up.

#9827. AI Made Us Faster. So Why Do Designers Have Less Time?

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

A poster that used to take me a day now takes a minute to generate. Last night I built an animated website in one evening without writing a single line of code. By every estimate, designers should have half their lives back.

Yet I haven't met a single designer who has more free time. Deadlines are shorter, revisions are longer, and by the evening there are so many options that your eyes start to blur.

So I tried to figure out what is going on. Are we bad at working with AI? Were we sold a fantasy? Or is this just a bubble that is about to pop? The answer turned out to be more interesting than all three.

In 2025, researchers at METR ran a simple experiment. Sixteen experienced developers worked on real tasks, some with AI tools and some without. Before they started, they expected AI to make them 24% faster.

With AI, tasks took 19% longer. The strangest part: even after the experiment, they believed AI had made them 20% faster.

The study is small, and it is about developers, not designers. But the same picture shows up in much larger surveys:

2,500 workers and executives in 4 countries

96% of executives expect AI to raise productivity. 77% of employees say it added to their workload

52 interviews, 300+ public AI initiatives

95% of organizations got zero return from generative AI

Computers went through the same thing in the 1980s. Economist Robert Solow famously observed that you could see the computer age everywhere except in the productivity statistics. The growth did come, but only after people rebuilt the way they worked.

I see three reasons, and none of them is that the models are bad.

1. Generation got cheap. Choosing didn't. A designer used to make three options and bring the best one. Now you can get 200 in an hour. Each one has to be looked at, compared, and rejected for a reason. Nobody counts that time, but it eats all the savings.

2. Clients know generation takes a minute too. So "by Friday" turned into "by tomorrow", and one round of revisions turned into five. Economists call this the Jevons paradox: when something gets cheaper, we consume more of it. Cheap images didn't reduce the work. They increased the appetite.

3. We dropped AI into the old process. Brief, references, sketches, approvals all stayed the same. There is just a new "generate" button in the middle. According to Upwork, 47% of employees using AI don't know how to reach the productivity gains their managers expect. And in the MIT report, the 5% of companies that succeeded rebuilt the process itself instead of buying one more tool.

There is one more thing METR showed. With AI, the feeling of speed and actual speed drift apart. Generating gives you the sense that work is happening even when it is stuck. For designers, it looks like an hour of rerolling one frame instead of five minutes thinking about what exactly is wrong with it.

Fair question. In June 2026, JPMorgan estimated global AI infrastructure spending at $5.5 trillion through 2030. The largest cloud providers alone are spending about $650 billion in 2026, increasingly with borrowed money. Investors argue about one thing: whether demand will catch up with the spending.

For designers, I think something else matters more. Even if the financial bubble pops, the tools won't disappear. After the dot-com crash in 2000, the internet didn't go away. The companies that couldn't make money on it did, and the ones that could grew in their place.

AI looks similar. If there is a bubble, it is in expectations: "buy a subscription and everything gets faster." The data above shows it doesn't work that way. But the change in the profession has already happened, and it won't roll back.

There is another tension in the industry. Open Threads and it looks like everyone is a designer now. The profession has ballooned and is changing in front of us. But behind a lot of those generations is a lack of basics: composition, grids, typography. AI doesn't fix that. It mass-produces it.

That is especially true for product designers moving from interfaces into visual work. A component library keeps a UI consistent, but there is no Storybook for light, texture and framing.

None of these steps requires a new model. They are all about who is running the process.

We weren't fooled. We were sold faster execution and assumed we had bought faster work. AI speeds up making things. It doesn't free up a designer's time on its own. The person who frees up time is the one who decided in advance what they are making and knows how to choose quickly.

That animated website from the first paragraph took one evening for exactly that reason: I knew what feeling I wanted before I typed the first prompt. Without that, I would still be rerolling it.

Has AI saved you time, or eaten it? And how have your deadlines changed in the last year?

AI Didn’t Kill Design. But Something About the Profession Is Changing Anyway

Art director and brand designer. Ex-Avito, ivi, MY.GAMES. Founder of Design Warm-ups, a 3,000+ designer community.

InfoQ Homepage News Claude Code Has Been Leaking Secrets through its "Don't Ask Again" Feature

Nov 22, 2026 2 min read

Agentic security firm Apiiro found that Claude Code has been exposing secrets in public repositories due to how it stores them in local file on developers' machines to implement the "Don't Ask Again" feature. The company identified 1,122 secrets in claude/settings.local.json files and another 1,160 in git history, in the shared settings.json intentionally committed, and in agent chat transcripts stored in repos.

The problem lies in how Claude Code handles command approval. When developers reply "Yes, and don’t ask again" to approve a shell command, Claude Code saves it as a permanent permission rule in the local configuration file .claude/settings.local.json, which may end up inadvertently containing embedded credentials, passwords and API tokens.

When [Claude Code] creates the file inside a git repo, it adds it to the developer's global git ignore list. That covers the common case. It doesn’t cover a folder that becomes a repo later, a clone on another machine, or a file someone already committed. The rule never goes into the repo's own .gitignore, so nothing travels with the project to protect it.

On some occasions, the researchers found, Claude Code itself committed the file. Overall 63 organizations were affected, with exposed secrets including cloud API keys, production passwords and access tokens, and npm tokens. Generic secret scanners such as gitleaks and TruffleHog failed to flag all exposed secrets, mostly because they were embedded inside shell commands.

The same password-in-a-command pattern appears wherever an agent records what it ran: transcripts, memory files, handoff notes, and a scanner tuned to key formats misses it in all of them.

The researches also note that the way Claude Code manages secrets is a security gap in itself, as to any malware "it’s a list of the systems the developer can reach and the passwords that open them, one file search away", available at the same path in every project.

Apiiro's findings were later reinforced by GitGuardian, which found 31,088 secrets in Claude Code’s .claude/settings.local.json on public GitHub, 5,343 of which were still valid at the time of detection, as well as another 613 in Docker Hub images. GitGuardian had previously warned that "Cursor, Claude Code, and GitHub Copilot leave credentials scattered across config files, logs, and shell history".

Commenting on the findings, Reddit user T_Thriller_T observed that "Somewhere, someone said AI companies are ignoring basic cyber security principles".

User MattV0 suggested an interesting approach to the whole matter of how to deal with AI files:

While this is about secrets, I totally stopped adding AI files into my projects. Means no settings, CLAUDE.md, AGENTS.md or anything else. I even turned off Claude's memory. [...] Nowadays I use a memory/task/docs server through mcp and it really improved such documentation issues.

At very very least, Apiiro recommends untracking the json file using git rm --cached .claude/settings.local.json and adding it to the repo's .gitignore, as well as rotating every credentials the file has ever contained. For a sounder approach, the researchers also recommend inspecting the file and deleting any rule that contains a secret, and avoid typing secrets directly into commands, referencing them instead through environment variables.

#9823. Build specialized multimodal models with LFM3

LFM3 is our new generation of Liquid Foundation Models (LFMs), built to be the starting point for specialized intelligence. It brings text, vision, audio, omni, and decision models onto one shared backbone, all in the 2B parameter range. This means you can pick the model for your modality, fine-tune it on your own data on a single GPU, and deploy it where your application runs.

LFM3 brings four main changes compared to our previous LFM2 family:

LFM2 showed that a hybrid of short convolutions and attention can run fast on-device without sacrificing quality. For LFM3, we used our hardware-in-the-loop architecture search to redesign that architecture for agentic use cases, which need more capability per parameter and fast inference over long contexts. The search now covers 14 device and backend combinations, from phones and a Raspberry Pi 5 to laptops, cloud CPUs, GPUs, and the Qualcomm Hexagon NPU.

LFM3-1.7B-Base has 24 layers and four main changes:

The payoff shows at long context. Per parameter, LFM3-1.7B matches LFM2-1.2B on short prompts across edge devices, and with 8K tokens in context it is about 25% faster. LFM3-1.7B-Base was pre-trained on 22T tokens with the same 128K vocabulary as LFM2.5-8B-A1B. The final 3.5T tokens are a mid-training stage on curated data with a larger share of agentic traces and tool calls, which also extends the context window to 256K tokens.

Every LFM3 model branches from LFM3-1.7B-Base. Instead of running one large general-purpose model, you pick the one that fits your inputs, customize it, and run it on-device.

The vision and audio models also get two new in-house encoders:

Each model runs in transformers. The snippets below come from the model cards, which also list the other inference engines each model supports.

Reach for LFM3-1.7B when you need local agents, tool calling, structured outputs, or a base for domain-specific fine-tuning. It is post-trained to run in agentic harnesses such as Hermes Agent, Pi, and OpenClaw. It outperforms its predecessor, LFM2.5-2.6B, with 35% fewer parameters, and the biggest gains are on agentic tasks: on WebArena-Verified, it scores 38.42 against 3.02, and it even beats Qwen3.5-9B on long tasks in browsers and business apps. You can find more details in the LFM3-1.7B model card.

To run LFM3-1.7B, install the latest version of transformers:

For local agent setup, see the Agent Harnesses guide.

Reach for LFM3-VL-2B when you need on-device visual understanding. It is the first LFM vision model that takes video as input; it reasons step by step before it answers, and it finds objects and reasons about how they are placed, a strong foundation for robotics. Compared with LFM2.5-VL-3B, it has fewer parameters (1.9B against 3.1B) yet raises the average across 62 vision benchmarks from 57.6 to 71.4, on par with Gemma 4 12B, a model more than six times larger. You can find more details in the LFM3-VL-2B model card.

To run LFM3-VL-2B, install transformers>=5.21.0 with its vision dependencies:

See the LFM3-VL-2B model card for tool calling, tool search, and on-device inference with llama.cpp.

Reach for LFM3-Audio-2B when you need voice chat, speech recognition, speech synthesis, or translation across 18 languages on a laptop or edge device. It takes text or audio as input and responds with text, speech, or both, and it can turn spoken requests into tool calls. Compared with LFM2.5-Audio-1.5B, it uses a new in-house audio encoder and speech codec, speaks with higher quality (UTMOSv2 3.83 against 3.22), and adds audio understanding, general-purpose audio reasoning, and tool calling. You can find more details in the LFM3-Audio-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Audio-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its audio dependencies:

Load the model and processor directly from the Hugging Face Hub:

Then ask a question aloud and get a reply in text and speech:

See the LFM3-Audio-2B model card for live speech recognition, speech synthesis, audio understanding, and tool calling.

Reach for LFM3-Omni-2B when you need one on-device model that sees, listens, and talks back, in place of a separate ASR model, vision-language model, LLM, and TTS model. It can answer spoken questions about an image, watch and listen to a video together, and turn what it sees and hears into tool calls. It is our first omni model, with text, vision, and audio input and both text and speech output, and it keeps the core capabilities of the standalone LFM3 models, including visual question answering, speech recognition, speech synthesis, and instruction following. Like LFM3-Audio-2B, it speaks through LiquidCodec, which turns generated tokens into speech faster than real time, so spoken replies stream as the model generates them. On audio-visual video understanding, it beats models up to 10.7B parameters, such as Qwen2.5-Omni-7B, on Daily-Omni, WorldSense, and AV-SpeakerBench. You can find more details in the LFM3-Omni-2B model card.

To run LFM3-Omni-2B, install transformers>=5.20.2 with its vision and audio dependencies:

Then ask a question about a photo by voice:

See the LFM3-Omni-2B model card for speech output, video with its soundtrack, and tool calling.

Reach for the d1 models when you need fast, structured decisions instead of generated text. Give them a situation (a support ticket, an invoice, an app screen, a photo, a voice note) and a list of questions, and they answer all of them in a single forward pass, each with a calibrated probability. Beyond yes/no, choices, and scores, they can now point at objects, read values from documents, estimate numbers with a range, and pick every option that applies. You can find more details in the model cards for d1-2B and d1-omni-2B.

To run d1-2B, install transformers>=5.19 with its vision dependencies:

Then load d1-2B and ask it several questions about one support ticket in a single pass:

For brevity, we only include the example for d1-2B. See the d1-omni-2B model card for audio clips and spoken questions.

LFM3 is built to be specialized. Frontier models are powerful generalists, but they are not necessarily experts in your use case. LFM3 packs extra capacity into a small, fast model, so a short fine-tune can turn it into a reliable expert on your task, with your data, terminology, and tools. Because it is small, you can deploy the fine-tuned model where your application runs, from devices to private infrastructure to the cloud.

Every model can be fine-tuned on a single GPU, and these notebooks walk you through a complete task for the text, vision, audio, and omni models, from data preparation to evaluation.

We adapt LFM3-VL-2B into three complementary robotics models for orchestration, navigation, and manipulation. The orchestrator operates a robot arm through tool calls: it grounds objects by pointing, measures them with depth tools, invokes motion planners, and checks outcomes in subsequent camera images. The navigator follows route descriptions using recent RGB observations, predicting spatial targets and a waypoint trajectory in just five tokens. The manipulation VLA maps images, language, and robot state to eight-step chunks of continuous actions in a single forward pass. Jointly trained across 15 embodiments, the VLA achieves 96.2% average success across the four LIBERO suites and 45.7% on RoboCasa-GR1 tabletop tasks, generating action chunks in under 50 ms on a Jetson AGX Orin with TensorRT FP16. These results highlight LFM3-VL-2B as a compact foundation for robotics, spanning high-level planning to low-level control with real-time action generation on embedded hardware.

Watch LFM3-VL-2B handle perception, navigation, and manipulation in this demo video.

All LFM3 models are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:

#9821. Optimizely Malware Attacks Highlight Third-Party Vendor Risks

At least 178 organizations, including several major brands, unwittingly exposed website visitors to hydra-like malware via a third-party platform.

Some of the world's most recognizable brands unwittingly became conduits for malware this week, after an attacker slipped malicious code into website testing scripts delivered by Optimizely, a platform that allows organizations to experiment with and optimize their online presence.

The attack potentially exposed visitors to sites operated by at least 178 organizations — including Zoom, CNN, Salesforce, and IKEA — to malware capable of stealing payment card details, hijacking cryptocurrency transactions, and delivering exploit kits for iPhones and iPads.

Many organizations use Optimizely to run website experiments, test different page designs and personalize content for visitors. To do this, Optimizely embeds scripts in customer websites that can serve different versions of a page or its content to visitors, track their interactions, and measure which versions perform best.

Related:What We Missed: Nvidia CEO Scandal Rocks AI Industry

The attackers appear to have exploited this mechanism to insert malicious code into a custom field called Project JavaScript, which allows Optimizely customers to run their own code across website pages.

British Web security monitoring service Report URI, among the first to detect the activity, documented the tampering but said it could not determine how the attackers gained the ability to modify customer projects. "We don't know how the attacker got write access to so many unrelated customer projects: a compromised Optimizely system, a compromised credential with cross-customer access, or something else. That's for Optimizely to explain," Report URL founder Scott Helme wrote.

Report URI said it located and examined 1,611 unique Optimizely scripts. It found malicious code in 188 scripts associated with 178 organizations. The company has published a list of the affected websites on its site, grouped by industry sector.

Optimizely itself has said little about the incident so far besides acknowledging it and pinning it somewhat vaguely to a vulnerability in the platform's Experimentation account sign-up flow. "We've fixed the vulnerability and removed the injected code from affected projects. We've also taken steps to secure affected user accounts and put additional protections in place to prevent unauthorized code from being delivered," the company said.

Related:Qwen Incidents Show Self-Hosted AI Models Need Stronger Steering

In a follow-up statement to Dark Reading, Optimizely spokesperson identified these measures as including "blocking access to the vulnerable path, deploying a fix, removing the injected code from affected projects, ending active sessions, revoking tokens, and resetting access for affected user accounts." The company has also implemented "additional protections to prevent malicious code from being delivered in Cloudflare. While the incident has been fully remediated, we are working with third-party experts on a comprehensive investigation," the statement read. Optimizely however, did not respond to a Dark Reading question on how a vulnerability in the account sign-up flow could have given an attacker write access to customer projects.

"That’s the question every affected customer should be putting to Optimizely right now," says Justin Beals, CEO and founder of Strike Graph. "They need to know how a new account got write access to other tenants' projects, which project IDs were changed and when, and whether that path is fully closed."

Until Optimizely explains the authorization failure, customers can't judge whether the company's reported fix addresses the cause or just the symptom, he says.

Related:Strike Graph Launches Integration AI to Automate Continuous Compliance Evidence Using Any Existing Tool

The incident is a reminder that organizations need strict controls over third-party scripts running on their websites, Beals adds. Most organizations approve a third-party vendor script once during procurement and never revisit it later. Optimizely, for instance, passed whatever review the 178 affected companies ran, and the malicious code still shipped from Optimizely's own CDN under its own certificate.

"The takeaway is that a vendor approval is a point-in-time decision, and the risk changes every time that vendor’s code changes," Beals says. "You can keep using these tools if you decide where they’re allowed to run."

Tyler Reguly, associate director of security R&D at Fortra, says incidents like these show why organizations implement a browser security feature called Subresource Integrity (SRI) to verify that externally hosted files, such as JavaScript, haven't been altered before they are loaded and executed.

"The problem that we have here is that you may include a file in your website that is safe for months or even years and then, unbeknownst to you, a breach occurs within your vendor and that 'file that's been safe forever' is suddenly no longer safe," Reguly says.

SRI allows organizations to perform version pinning based on file hashes to protect against attacks like the one that went down at Optimizely. "The downside is that it requires a bit more effort and management to maintain your Web pages, which are often seen as 'set it and forget it' resources," Reguly adds.

Chris Nyhuis, CEO of Vigilant, says Optimizely demonstrates what happens when trust becomes an attack surface. "Organizations allowed a third party to deliver executable code into their customers' browsers, and that trust was exploited," he says.

The answer isn't to eliminate third-party technology but to eliminate "blind trust," Nyhuis says. "Restrict where vendor scripts execute, limit their access to sensitive data, monitor their behavior and changes, and independently validate what they're doing."

Furthermore, Optimizely also needs to explain how a flaw in an account sign-up process allowed an attacker to modify executable code belonging to 178 unrelated customers. "For that to happen, there had to be a path around customer authorization boundaries," he says. "Whether that involved broken tenant isolation, privilege escalation, an authorization flaw, or access to an overly privileged service remains to be established by the forensic investigation."

This article was updated at 1 p.m. ET on Nov. 18 to reflect a statement from Optimizely.

Illinois-based Jai Vijayan is a veteran, award-winning technology journalist with more than 25 years of experience covering cybersecurity. His information security reporting has explored everything from ransomware, nation-state threats, and identity security to AI risk, critical infrastructure protection, software supply chain security, cloud security and emerging enterprise technologies.

Over the course of his career, Jai has written news stories, feature articles, survey reports, white papers, and e-books for enterprise and technology audiences. He has also moderated panel discussions and executive roundtables featuring CISOs, security researchers, and industry leaders.

His work has earned multiple industry honors, including a Joint ASBPE Excellence Award for Best Coverage of Government IT, and a Joint Jesse H. Neal Award for wireless LAN security coverage. Jai holds a Master’s degree in statistics from Bangalore University, and studied broadcasting and electronic communication at Marquette University in Milwaukee.

#9819. Setting Up AWS Control Tower? These SCP and Networking Mistakes Can Cost You Hours

Most landing-zone guides stop after "click Set up landing zone". This one keeps going. By the end, you will have a working multi-account AWS environment where every account has one job, the rules are enforced by Service Control Policies, and the network is owned by one account and shared with the others. Each rule is tested from the command line, so you can prove it holds.

Everything here was built in a real organization, including the parts that went wrong: an SCP that broke DNS, an "allow list" SCP that allowed everything, and a RAM share that failed for 40 minutes. The fixes are part of the steps and are collected in the Troubleshooting section.

This is part 1 of a series. Part 2 sets up the Build account (CodeCommit, ECR with cross-account pull, and CodeBuild inside the shared VPC), and part 3 runs the application on ECS in Dev and Production.

Seven accounts, grouped into Organizational Units (OUs), each with one responsibility:

The "must not" rules matter as much as ownership: each one becomes a Deny statement in an SCP, so it holds even for an administrator inside that account.

An AWS account is a hard boundary for IAM permissions, billing, service quotas, and the blast radius of mistakes. When dev, prod, networking, and CI/CD share one account, a developer who needs the dev cluster easily ends up with access to production, and costs can only be split with careful tagging. Separate accounts give you these boundaries for free, and OUs let you apply the same rules to a group of accounts at once: every account you add to the Workloads OU later inherits its guardrails.

The design follows one principle, ownership: for any resource, it should be obvious which account owns it and who is allowed to change it. The network belongs to the Network account, images belong to the Build account, and the running application belongs to the workload account. Images are built once and only pulled by Dev and Production, so Production runs exactly what was tested in Dev.

This article builds only Dev and Production. A Staging account can be added later in exactly the same way.

Control Tower itself is free, but the services it enables are not. Approximate monthly costs in eu-central-1 for this setup:

The NAT gateways are almost all of the bill. If you build this only to learn, follow the Cleanup section when you are done, or delete the NAT gateways between sessions.

Control Tower creates the organization structure, the two shared accounts in the Security OU, an organization-wide CloudTrail trail, and AWS Config in every enrolled account. Everything later in this article builds on it.

Before you start: if IAM Identity Center is already enabled in the management account, Control Tower must be set up in the same Region. Choose the home Region carefully. Changing it later means decommissioning the landing zone.

Sign in to the management account and open AWS Control Tower → Set up landing zone.

On the first page, choose your home Region and Automatic account enrollment. With automatic enrollment, accounts that join the organization later (and accounts you move between OUs) get the Control Tower baseline and controls without manual enrollment.

On the second page, keep the recommended Sandbox OU. It is a place for experiments with fewer restrictions, and we will also use it to test new SCPs before they reach other OUs.

Next, Control Tower asks for the two shared accounts in the Security OU:

The setup takes about 35 minutes. You can follow each step on the landing zone page:

Control Tower created the Security and Sandbox OUs. Create the other three under Root in Control Tower → Organization → Create resources → Create organizational unit: Infrastructure, Deployments, and Workloads. Create them through Control Tower, not the Organizations console, so that they are registered and get the Control Tower controls.

If you expect many workloads, you can nest OUs later, for example Workloads/web and Workloads/ai, and attach different policies to each.

Use Control Tower → Account Factory → Create account for each workload account:

Account Factory provisions accounts one at a time, so creating all four takes a while. When it's done, Control Tower → Organization should show every OU as Registered and every account as Enrolled:

Control Tower configures IAM Identity Center. It creates groups such as AWSControlTowerAdmins, AWSSecurityAuditors, and AWSLogArchiveViewers, and permission sets such as AWSAdministratorAccess, AWSPowerUserAccess, and AWSReadOnlyAccess. In every enrolled account, your user gets AWSAdministratorAccess directly, while the AWSControlTowerAdmins group only gets AWSOrganizationsFullAccess. That direct assignment is how I sign in everywhere in this article:

For a team, don't give everyone administrator access. Create groups by role and assign each group only to the accounts it needs:

In the console: IAM Identity Center → Groups → Create group, then AWS accounts → select the accounts → Assign users or groups → choose the group and the permission set. The same assignment from the CLI:

For the command line, add one profile per account to ~/.aws/config, then sign in once with aws sso login --sso-session lz. One sign-in covers all profiles:

Tip: use the role name that you actually see in the access portal. In my organization the management account has AdministratorAccess while member accounts have AWSAdministratorAccess. A wrong role name fails with "ForbiddenException: No access".

Also check that no AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID or AWS_SESSION_TOKEN environment variables are set in your shell. The CLI uses them whenever a command has no --profile, so a single forgotten flag silently runs that command against a completely different account. I had exactly this situation, with keys for an unrelated organization in my shell.

Service Control Policies (SCPs) are guardrails in AWS Organizations. They define the maximum permissions available to IAM users and roles in the accounts of an OU, regardless of what their IAM policies allow.

We use them to enforce the Region, to block dangerous actions (leaving the organization, disabling security services), to enforce ownership (only the Network account builds connectivity), and to remove risky shortcuts (root user, long-lived access keys). SCPs say "what's possible", IAM policies say "who can do it".

We don't attach our policies to the Security OU. Control Tower manages the Audit and Log Archive accounts and already protects them with its own guardrails (the aws-guardrails-* policies you can see in the list).

Every Deny statement below has an exception for the AWSControlTowerExecution role and the stacksets-exec-* roles. Control Tower uses these roles to manage the accounts, and blocking them would break enrollment and drift repair.

Go to AWS Organizations → Policies → Service control policies → Create policy, and name it BaselineGuardrails :

The Network account owns connectivity. FullAWSAccess already allows that, so we only add what it must not do: run applications or CI/CD.

The Build account owns pipelines and container images. It must not create its own network connectivity (Transit Gateway, peering, VPN, Direct Connect) and must not run application services or databases.

Dev and Production run the application. They may attach their VPC to a Transit Gateway shared by the Network account, but cannot build their own connectivity, create ECR repositories, push images, or create pipelines. Images are built once in the Build account and only pulled here.

Select the policy → Actions → Attach policy, and choose the OU:

Leave FullAWSAccess attached. Our policies only take permissions away from it.

The final picture for the Workloads OU should be: FullAWSAccess, the Control Tower aws-guardrails-* policy, BaselineGuardrails, and WorkloadsECSPolicy:

Always test SCPs right after attaching them. EC2 supports --dry-run, which checks permissions without creating anything:

The error message names the exact SCP that denied the request, which makes troubleshooting much easier. Section 7 has a script that tests all guardrails at once.

Tip: before attaching a new SCP to a production OU, attach it to the Sandbox OU or a test account first. A wrong Deny statement affects every account in the OU immediately.

With the guardrails in place, we can build the network. The Network account owns all VPCs, subnets, route tables, NAT gateways, and internet gateways. Dev, Production, and Build don't create VPCs. They receive subnets from the Network account through AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM).

One shared VPC for everyone would put Dev and Production on the same network. Instead, each environment gets its own VPC, shared only with its own account, and we don't need a Transit Gateway yet.

Before creating anything, plan the IP ranges. VPCs that may need to be connected later (with Transit Gateway or peering) must not overlap. Control Tower created a VPC in every account with the same 172.31.0.0/16 range, and these VPCs can never be connected to each other.

We reserve a /16 range for each environment:

Each environment VPC uses two Availability Zones and three subnet tiers:

The app subnets are larger (/20, about 4,000 addresses) because every ECS task on Fargate gets its own IP address. Production uses the same layout with 10.20.x.x. The build VPC needs only two public and two private subnets (10.30.0.0/24, 10.30.1.0/24, 10.30.16.0/20, 10.30.32.0/20).

Control Tower's Account Factory created an empty VPC named aws-controltower-VPC in every new account. We don't need them, so delete them in the Network, Build, Dev, and Production accounts (VPC → Your VPCs → select aws-controltower-VPC → Actions → Delete VPC).

To prevent Control Tower from creating these VPCs in future accounts, go to Control Tower → Account Factory → Network configuration → Edit, and set the maximum number of private subnets to 0.

Sign in to the Network account, open VPC → Create VPC, and choose VPC and more. This wizard creates the VPC, subnets, route tables, internet gateway, NAT gateway, and VPC endpoints in one step.

Expand Customize subnets CIDR blocks and enter the CIDRs from the table above. The wizard's defaults would give the public subnets /20 ranges, which wastes addresses we want to keep for ECS tasks.

ECS tasks in private subnets need outbound access to pull container images, send logs, and call external APIs. This is the job of the NAT gateway. The wizard offers three options:

We make a different choice per environment:

For prod, choose Regional instead of Zonal. There is no AZ selection for a regional NAT gateway, because AWS manages its availability across zones:

Choose S3 Gateway. Gateway endpoints are free. Amazon ECR stores image layers in S3, so most of the traffic when ECS pulls an image goes through the endpoint instead of the NAT gateway, which reduces NAT data processing costs.

We don't create interface endpoints (ECR, CloudWatch Logs, STS) yet. At about $0.01 per hour per AZ each, five of them in two AZs cost more than the NAT gateway they would replace.

Keep DNS hostnames and DNS resolution enabled.

Before creating the VPC, check the Preview panel on the right. It shows every resource the wizard will create. You should see six subnets, one internet gateway, one NAT gateway, and private route tables with a 0.0.0.0/0 route to the NAT gateway.

Click Create VPC. Creating the NAT gateway takes a minute or two.

Open the VPC and look at the Resource map tab. It shows the whole design on one screen: six subnets in two AZs, the public route table pointing to the internet gateway, and the private route tables pointing to the NAT gateway and the S3 endpoint.

Repeat the same steps for prod (10.20.0.0/16, Regional NAT gateway) and build (10.30.0.0/16, 2 public and 2 private subnets, Zonal NAT gateway in 1 AZ).

First, allow RAM to share resources within the organization. In the management account, open Resource Access Manager → Settings and enable Enable sharing with AWS Organizations. Without this setting, resources can only be shared through invitations.

Now, in the Network account, open Resource Access Manager → Resource shares → Create resource share:

When I created the first share, it failed with this error, even though organization sharing was enabled a few minutes earlier:

The message suggests waiting for onboarding to finish, but mine still failed after 40 minutes, from every account. The real hint came from the CLI: sharing with the organization as principal returned UnknownResourceException: Organization o-xxxxxxxx. RAM had never imported the organization, even though the Organizations console listed RAM as a trusted service.

The fix was to reset RAM trusted access from the management account:

Run this only before you have any resource shares. Disabling trusted access affects existing organization-based shares. After the reset, sharing worked within a minute.

Before that, I ruled out our own SCP by detaching BaselineGuardrails from the Infrastructure OU for a minute. A good habit in a governed account: rule out your own SCPs first. The error message names the denying SCP, as in this example where the region lock blocks CloudTrail in us-east-1:

Sign in to the Dev account and open VPC → Subnets. The shared subnets appear with the Network account as the owner.

Guardrails are easy to get subtly wrong, so I keep a script that checks the important rules in one run. It only uses read-only calls and EC2 --dry-run, so it never creates anything:

The "allow" checks matter too: a guardrail that blocks too much is also a bug, like my first region lock that broke Route 53. Run the script after every SCP change.

Every problem I hit while building this part, in one place:

If you built this only to learn, delete it in this order. Participants must remove their resources from shared subnets before the owner can delete them.

Dev, Production, and Build accounts: delete anything you launched into the shared subnets, including security groups.

Network account: delete the three RAM shares. Then delete the NAT gateways and release their Elastic IP addresses (this stops most of the cost), and delete the three VPCs.

Management account: detach and delete the four custom SCPs. To remove everything, decommission the landing zone in Control Tower, then close the member accounts. Closed accounts stay suspended for 90 days.

We now have a landing zone where every account has one clear job, and the boundaries are enforced rather than just documented:

#9818. Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Breaking cybersecurity news, news analysis, commentary, and other content from around the world, with an initial focus on the Middle East & Africa, the Asia Pacific, Europe, and Latin America.

Government-sanctioned authentication middleware is used for exceptionally important legal documents, yet it's often rife with RCE bugs.

Brazil's digital certificate system was recently found to be rife with vulnerabilities in browser extensions used by millions of government agencies and legal, medical, and tax professionals.

That's the assessment of researchers at Bay Area Labs, who this week flagged five particularly popular digital extensions that allow Brazilian citizens and institutions to not only sign official documents, but sign them with the greatest possible degree of trust issued by their government. All five of them possessed vulnerabilities which could've allowed attacker-controlled websites to run arbitrary code on users' machines.

One can only hope that the researchers, who disclosed the vulnerabilities this week, were the first to discover them. Remote code execution (RCE) in this context could have allowed fraudsters to sign legal documents in victims' names, and hackers to breach major government organizations (as well as professionals who manage large amounts of personal, financial, tax, and health information on behalf of their clients).

Related:Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

On Sept. 23, 2020, Brazil's National Congress enacted Federal Law No. 14,063. 14,063 laid the ground rules on how individuals and organizations could digitally sign documents when dealing with public institutions. Among other things, it delineated three tiers of trust that an electronic signature could carry: "simple," "advanced," and "qualified." "Qualified" meant that a digital signature would be equivalent to a notarized, handwritten one. It would be sufficient for high-stakes legal proceedings, like real estate transfers and electronic tax processes. And any digital signature backed with an ICP-Brasil certificate — ICP-Brasil is the country's official national public key infrastructure (PKI) framework — would be considered "qualified."

Brazilian government institutions, tax professionals, and anyone in-between who wants to provide a qualified digital signature for a sensitive legal document online can use browser extensions like Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital. Each of these tools lets official government and vendor portals read ICP-Brasil certificates, to confirm that signers are who they say they are, and put pen to Web page.

These tools will also engage with non-official websites. So if an attacker can lure a victim to their own site — or, in some cases, plant a malicious ad or iframe on a legitimate site — they can engage that victim's authentication middleware. Only one of the five extensions, CertiPlugin, had any kind of allowlist, yet it included any domain ending in ".one," meaning that an attacker would simply need to purchase a domain with that common and freely available suffix in order to perform an attack.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

The core issue endemic to each of these five extensions, and others used by other national governments, is that they allow websites to dictate the dynamic link libraries (DLLs) they load. Loading cryptographic libraries is a normal part of the way these apps work. But if they don't properly check that a loaded file is trusted? In that case, an attacker that lures a victim to their site can trigger a malware download and then instruct the victim's signing software to load that malware as if it were a legitimate library.

All five extensions' RCE vulnerabilities earned "critical" 9.6 scores in the Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS). Each of them was patched as of mid-September, but lessons remain.

Lacuna Web PKI, Softplan Web Signer, Certisign WebSigner, Certisign CertiPlugin, and BRy Assinatura Digital have more than 10 million installs between them.

Among that user base are some of the most significant, high-value organizations and professionals in the country. On its website, Lacuna alone counts Brazil's Federal Senate, its National Council of Justice, its navy, and its stock exchange among its clients "who trust our work." These extensions are far from limited to major government agencies, of course. BRy advertises its work with the University of São Paulo, the São Paulo metro, and one of the country's few biggest banks, Caixa Econômica Federal.

Related:Google Project Zero Slashes Bug Disclosure Deadlines, Splitting Experts

Attackers could have used the vulnerable authentication middleware to infect employees at major state institutions and, in Arnott's words, "cause mayhem." As an easier alternative, they could target middle class professionals: lawyers, doctors, accountants and so on. An accountant might manage digital signing credentials for hundreds of different individuals and businesses on their single computer. An attacker with that accountant's access could then impersonate those people and companies in legally significant transactions — forging agreements, submitting false tax filings ... the sky's the limit.

"It's really interesting how these signing tools always consistently have the same critical vulnerabilities," Arnott marvels, after having found characteristically similar vulnerabilities in extensions used by Belgium, Sweden, and Qatar's governments in recent months. "Since they are security tools, you'd expect them to be properly built. But they're so often making the same mistake, by allowing any site to pick which DLLs to load. I imagine it's to reduce friction so organizations can more easily load in the drivers for hardware security tokens and readers, because the driver DLLs aren't always known to the signing tool vendor or signed properly with Authenticode. It is insane to me how many independent vendors make this same mistake though."

Nate Nelson is a journalist and award-winning scriptwriter. In addition to Dark Reading he writes for Darknet Diaries, the most popular show in cybersecurity across all media.

He began his career as a freelancer, ghostwriting Forbes and CNBC op-eds for executives in tech and finance. Then he transitioned to journalism at Threatpost, where he covered cybersecurity news and trends. Throughout those years he co-created a cybersecurity podcast, Malicious Life, which in its day climbed into the Top 20 technology podcasts charts on Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

He holds degrees from New York University and Bard College. As a born and bred New Yorker, he enjoys a superiority complex, but is polite enough to keep it to himself.
