#9773. Navigating Vulnerability Hysteria in the AI Era

Cybersecurity In-Depth: Feature articles on security strategy, latest trends, and people to know.

This installment of the Reporters' Notebook video series examines the fallout from recent high-severity flaw disclosures, exploring how fears of AI-assisted exploits trigger widespread panic, operational disruptions, and growing warning fatigue.

The pressure on cybersecurity teams to patch critical vulnerabilities is reaching a boiling point, exacerbated by incessant coverage and rapid-fire disclosures of AI-discovered bugs. Last month, it was PHP2Shell. This week, it's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938), a 9.2 CVSS flaw in OpenJDK's Base64 decoder unearthed in just one hour using OpenAI's Codex by Calif Research, and NGINX2Root (CVE-2026-123007), a 9.2 CVSS critical integer underflow vulnerability affecting nginx HTTP/2 discovered by Rapid7 MDR.

In the latest installment of the monthly Reporters' Notebook video series, TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei, Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones, and Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid discuss last month's PHP2Shell vulnerability and examine whether the industry is falling victim to communal panic.

PHP2Shell refers to two critical PHP vulnerabilities — CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 — discovered by Calif (the same company that found Java4Shell) and rated 9.2 on the CVSS scale. Caused by out-of-memory corruption and stale global state errors, the flaws enable unauthenticated remote attackers to execute arbitrary code on Web servers without requiring credentials or prior access. Following a rocky, coordinated disclosure process marked by accidental leaks on X, many organizations preemptively pulled websites and critical services offline, fearing that threat actors leveraging AI would rapidly launch automated attacks before Web servers and applications could be patched.

Related:NIST Enrichment Reductions Impact CVE Coverage, Accuracy

However, the anticipated wave of machine-speed exploits failed to immediately materialize during "Black October," raising questions about whether extreme preemptive shutdowns do more harm than good. While AI accelerates vulnerability discovery, complex exploit paths, hardware dependencies, and flawed proof-of-concept code mean that severe flaws do not automatically lead to immediate compromises, even when attackers use AI. Constantly shuttering operations or broadcasting catastrophes can create early-warning fatigue, akin to ignored national weather alerts, leaving organizations numb when a genuine emergency strikes.

A similar wave of urgency currently surrounds Java4Shell, where researchers demonstrated unauthenticated remote code execution in widely deployed enterprise tools like Keycloak and Jenkins, prompting CISA to call for immediate patching. However, Java4Shell does not have a universal exploit, meaning attackers must consider each application's memory layout and timing, how Base64 is used, and take application-dependent steps to exploit it.

Related:Java4Shell Flaw Threatens Global Enterprises, Java Application Ecosystem

A CISO's primary responsibility is not to unilaterally order costly operational shutdowns or carry sole accountability for business risk, but to clearly communicate technical an,,,m d operational risks to executive leadership equipped to weigh security threats against business continuity. Staying calm, focusing on risk-based prioritization, and adhering to core security fundamentals remain the most effective defenses against modern threats.

Learn more in the video, and also check out other Reporters' Notebook episodes, available here, for insights and coverage from across Informa TechTarget's network of cybersecurity sister sites.

This transcript has been edited for clarity, readability, and length by Informa TechTarget's internal AI assistant and human editors. For the full experience, please watch the video.

Dark Reading's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Hi, and welcome to this month's installment of Reporters' Notebook, featuring reporters from Dark Reading, TechTarget Cybersecurity, and Cybersecurity Dive. I'm Fahmida Rashid, editor-in-chief of Dark Reading. This month, we are going to be talking about scary security vulnerabilities and the lessons we should take about how they're disclosed. So, joining me are Alyssa and Dave.

Related:Major Brazilian Signature Apps Enable RCE & Fraud

Why don't you introduce yourself quickly before we start the topic?

TechTarget Cybersecurity's Alissa Irei: Sure. I'm Alissa Irei, senior reporter with TechTarget, covering cybersecurity news.

Cybersecurity Dive's David Jones: David Jones. I'm a reporter at Cybersecurity Dive

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: All right, let's get started. We had what researchers have been calling PHP2Shell, which were essentially two security vulnerabilities found in some versions of PHP. In some software, using PHP is pretty serious. We're talking memory corruption, the ability to run code on a Web server without logging in.NNNNNNNNNN

We know it was serious and pretty scary because, on the CVSS score, it was a 9.2 out of 10. That's pretty big news. And whenever you tell anyone that by exploiting vulnerabilities, an attacker will be able to run their code on the Web server without logging in, it gets people worried. I believe the patches were out. There was a whole coordinated disclosure.

TTC's Alissa Irei: This struck me as a pretty big deal. Our colleague James Walker wrote a couple of articles on the vulnerabilities themselves and also the disclosure process, which I believe got a little bit rocky in terms of accidental early disclosures on X, and then there was a lot of racing to patch and companies taking their websites down. But yeah, PHP is in use, in, I think, 70% of the world's websites.

Anything that enables remote code execution seems like a really big deal to me. So, I thought it was noteworthy. I know, Dave, your take seems to be a little bit "this meeting could have been an email." Maybe when all is said and done, it was somewhat overblown.

CD's David Jones: I thought it was absolute chaos. I'm still trying to understand exactly what happened last month because the initial rollout of the patch, the disclosure, as you mentioned, was more than a little rocky and the hype around the entire situation in terms of what was actually at risk. That was kind of a bit of a moving target.

We've had situations in the past where there's a lot of concern that you're going to have what is considered systemic risk on such a global scale that large institutions will not be able to manage that risk in a timely manner. Obviously, there are a couple of factors that kind of played into this.

One was the fact that AI was involved in the discovery. With the fact that malicious actors are able to exploit vulnerabilities faster than they ever have been before. There's a great deal of concern in terms of are you able to address these vulnerabilities in a fast-enough method to get those patched, tested, and verified before malicious actors have a chance to attack them? I think what we saw last month was just a lot of preemptive action where major institutions all over the world were basically preemptively taking their sites offline because they had no way of triaging the potential fallout in time to properly address whether or not they were fully protected.

It's still a bit of a mystery to me exactly what happened, whether there was an initial overreaction, whether there were elements of the exploit that we just didn't understand. There was a lot of bad code in a lot of the proofs of concept, and it just never quite amounted to the emergency that it was set up to be.

Maybe it was a good exercise. But we're still trying to get to the bottom of exactly what took place and how we can avoid some of the exaggerated threat that we saw.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: You brought up two really important things that I want to make sure we dig into. The first one was, there was a bit of a fear that because the adversaries have AI, we don't know how fast they're going to be able to launch an attack. And I think that was the reason for some of this panic … you know, take down the website so that we have time to figure it out.

With Log4j, what was it, three days before we started seeing proofs of concept? And I think there was this sense that we don't have those three days anymore. I think, Dave, you make a really good point that maybe this was a good exercise. Maybe we now know that at least for now, it will not be the same day. We're not going to see an attack the day we see the vulnerability.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Well, the tricky thing about that, though, is can we say that? Because AI can move so quickly, it can also move much more slowly than we anticipate. But is today the day? I do think that there's a big question mark around, you know, sophisticated machine-speed AI-enabled attacks that we're not seeing yet. But also, you don't want to be the organization that is the Wikipedia entry for the big one.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Yes. That's true. But I definitely do think that part of that entire response was driven with we don't know when those attacks were coming. But, Dave, you also noted a second point which I thought was really interesting. That even with AI, the exploit path was a lot more complicated to exploit. I think we've always said in our beat that just because there is a vulnerability, just because there is a way to exploit, does not mean it will automatically be exploited. Sometimes the process to do it is hard, and not all attackers are going to take that harder route. And I think this was an example.

CD's David Jones: I think, you know, in a way it's good that we're thinking about how we respond to these types of things. Maybe we're better prepared, but at the same time, I think we don't want to get into a situation where we're crying wolf ahead of time. And at the end of the day, what actually happened?

Was Black October deserved? I mean, was it really that bad a month? Because I've seen worse.

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good point. It reminds me of, you know, national disaster weather warnings. At some point, if you go through enough of them and nothing much happens, people become inclined to ignore them. And at some point, that can be quite dangerous. So, I think it's a fair point.

Do you think that this sort of … I think we used the word hysteria in a previous conversation, communal hysteria, if you will. Do you think that this is specific to the AI age? It has this tendency to overreact. Has it grown in the age of AI and given us our fears about adversarial AI, or do you think that this is a pre-existing tendency that we as an industry have?

CD's David Jones: When you're a security team, particularly a security team with limited resources, you can't respond to every critical flaw or even medium- or high-severity flaw.

Whenever you want to, the resource is not there. You have to prioritize; you have to make decisions about the vulnerabilities that are going to affect the most critical technology.

Can I take the proper steps to either slow this process down or stop it before it gets out of control and I lose control over exactly how my operation continues? Because you have certain businesses where you may be operating in an OT environment where you can't afford to shut down for a certain amount of time. You may be running a hospital; you might be running a factory. You might be running fuel through a pipeline. You can't necessarily afford to be offline for a certain amount of time.

It's a difficult thing. I mean, there are probably a lot of organizations that were basically shut down for a certain amount of time, and they lost money, they lost time, they lost productivity. I don't think we can do that each and every time there's a critical situation.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: That's actually the one thing that occurred to me, when Web people were like, we need to take the site down while we figure things out. And I was like, just a couple of weeks prior, we had people taking down their Citrix boxes because there was a vulnerability and we didn't know what was going on. We don't know what's going on, so turn it off. And to Dave's point, we can't turn everything off. So, it's getting to be a priority, but to also understand when something is so bad that it is a turning-off incident. Because I'm worried that we're kind of moving into this state of turning it off every time, and that's just not practical.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: One thing I want to make sure we get a chance to talk about, and I love that Dave mentioned Log4j, because I think it's one of the biggest concerns. So, with Log4j, as a refresher for everyone, it was a vulnerability in a logging framework used by Java applications. And the challenge was that it's used in all sorts of different applications. And so, you could be like, nope, I looked, but I don't have Log4j, not realizing your suppliers were using it. And I think there was a bit of a worry that this might be the same, where I might not be using it, but I don't know who else is.

Which I think is a very legitimate concern. You need to know not just what you have, what your suppliers have, what your partners have. And I think that was the one aspect of PHP2Shell that kind of got a little obscure. That entire concept of thinking broader and bigger is something that really reminded me with this one that vulnerabilities are not just in your stuff; they're in other people's stuff too.

TTC's Alissa Irei: I think it's a great point. And I do worry about the smaller open source projects that have one or two maintainers, and it seems like everyone is drowning in vulnerabilities these days. And what does that mean for teams that are barely teams, and what does that mean for the software supply chain? I think it's a legitimate worry.

CD's David Jones: I'm not sure that a CISO or a frontline security operations team has the authority to take anything out of service without having a conversation higher up the food chain. I mean, you've got to be in a situation where … let's say there's an emergency, you've got to have people kind of above your pay grade where you have conversations where, yeah, we're not going to be producing food for the next few days, maybe. Or we've got to stop these surgeries if you're in a hospital system. The nuclear plant is not going to be, you know, cooling down for maybe a few hours. You've got to have this thought out in terms of, OK, can you explain to somebody who may not be a trained engineer, who may not be versed in these various systems, why you have to move forward and disrupt the entire business operation for a certain amount of time, because if you let it continue, and let's say somebody gets into your IT environment or your OT environment, and you may not be able to see them.

Are you willing to take that risk? Are you going to be held responsible for taking that risk? And who's going to be the C-suite person or the operational leader whoever makes that call that's going to say, "Yeah, go ahead and pull the plug"?

TTC's Alissa Irei: It's a good reminder that ultimately a CISO's job in some of these cases is communicating risk, not deciding how to manage the risk. Because if I'm a CISO, I wouldn't want to be making that decision about shutting down a hospital or a nuclear power plant. It becomes about being able to quickly and accurately communicate the operational risk to someone who is paid to make those decisions.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: We're increasingly seeing situations where the CISO is the one left holding the bag. So yeah, it's definitely a bigger calculation. To Alyssa's point, communicate it; make sure everyone understands what this means so that it's an informed decision.

TTC's Alissa Irei: Actually, this makes me think of two comments that have come up in recent conversations. One was with an analyst who said the CISO's job is and has always been to manage risk to the best of their ability and then take the blame when things go wrong. And she was very clear that that has not changed in the age of AI; it is the continuation of a pattern.

You know, debatable, but on some days I'm sure that feels true if you're a CISO. Another conversation I had recently was about CISO risk and the need for … I think there's some growing murmurs in the CISO community about the need to push back on the risk that is not actually security's bag to hold and be a little bit more vocal and clear about offloading some of that risk to people who are really better equipped and paid to hold it.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: I think overall it's worth saying that yes, this is serious, yes, this is huge, here's a priority list. But you know what? Maybe it is the time to be a little bit contrarian.

Dave, what would you say is the one lesson you want our listeners, our readers, to be taking away?

CD's David Jones: Well, I guess the question I would have is: Are you prepared and properly set up to address such a situation the next time it happens, because it might happen over Thanksgiving.

Let's agree that AI has the ability to find critical flaws that might take a human team days, weeks, or months to find.

There are state actors and sophisticated criminal actors that can get access to an AI-assisted or automated attack. Find out how to best attack a vulnerability. That could happen within the space of days or hours.

You can't have a team on standby 24/7 all the time responding to every alarm that goes off. It's not cost-effective. It's unrealistic. But to be fair, you have to be prepared to respond to that in some way.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: Definitely. Alissa, what would you say yours would be?

TTC's Alissa Irei: Mine is much broader and much less useful.

I think I saw it on a tea towel somewhere, but stay calm and look for signs. I think that's what I'm trying to do. I don't really have a good handle on where this is going next. I don't know that anybody does. So, it seems like that's the best that any security team can do. You know, focus on risk, focus on potential impact and prioritizing actions based on that. And in the meantime, to Dave's point, we'll try to avoid communal hysteria and do what we can do when we can do it, as fast as we can do it, and as smartly as we can do it. And I think that's all anybody can ask because, you know, we've never been here before.

DR's Fahmida Y. Rashid: My thought was kind of similar to yours, that the fundamentals still matter. Know what you're securing, keep an eye on how you're working, you know, keeping an eye on your alerts. Yes, everything is a little new because we're now kind of in this age of, you know, things are being found more complicated, faster, but it's still the fundamentals, right? We need to know what we have so that we can secure it quickly and efficiently communicate it. To Dave's point, let's hope that we don't have these kinds of disastrous months every single month because I don't think we're going to be able to keep up with that volume

So, I'm going to say thank you so much for joining me for this month's Reporters' Notebook. I hope you enjoyed the conversation as much as I did. And see you next month.

Fahmida Y. Rashid is an award-winning B2B cybersecurity journalist with over two decades of experience covering enterprise technology. As editor-in-chief, she leads Dark Reading's editorial strategy. In her reporting and writing, she focuses on the following areas: application security; cloud, network, and infrastructure security; identity and access management; third-party and supply chain risk; governance and compliance; and cybersecurity data analytics.

Past leadership roles include Executive Editor at VentureBeat, where she led the newsroom's transition to focus editorially on AI and data technologies; co-founder of the cybersecurity magazine Decipher; and serving as founding editor-in-chief of the RSAC Conference. Her work has appeared in various business and tech trade publications, including CSO Online, InfoWorld, and eWEEK. Prior to specializing in information security, she covered enterprise IT, especially networking, open source software, and core internet infrastructure at Forbes.com and CRN. She also reviewed networking technologies as an analyst at CRN Test Center and PCMag. She began her career writing financial briefs at Women's Wear Daily.

Before becoming a journalist, she spent over 10 years as an IT professional and has experience as a network administrator, database administrator, software developer, management consultant, and product manager.

Fahmida Y. Rashid holds a master's degree in journalism and a certificate in computational journalism from Columbia University Graduate School of Journalism. #9772. Comparing Qini, IPW, and Doubly Robust Metrics for Uplift Modeling

Staff Data Scientist at Careem. Writing about causal inference, experimentation, and practical AI—from model assumptions to real decisions.

Staff Data Scientist at Careem. Writing about causal inference, experimentation, and practical AI—from model assumptions to real decisions.

Staff Data Scientist at Careem. Writing about causal inference, experimentation, and practical AI—from model assumptions to real decisions.

Why causal estimation needs causal evaluation, and how Inverse Propensity Weighting and Doubly Robust scores change model comparisons

What if your uplift metric ranked an imperfect model above the true treatment-effect ranking? In a simulation where we know the answer, Qini can do exactly that, and following its recommendation means choosing a ranking with lower true causal gain.

Let’s start with the classical uplift problem. Suppose a company needs to decide which customers of theirs to send marketing messages to. The best ranking of customers would be based on the expected benefit from sending them a marketing message, which depends on the value of the action we try to nudge them to and the shift in the probability of performing this action due to the receiving the communication. Of course, the company doesn’t know these probabilities, so it uses an imperfect ranking based on their estimates.

Let’s take a hypothetical situation in which we know the real probabilities, that means we know the real perfect ranking of the customers in terms of the efficiency of communication. Suppose we decided to compare it with the imperfect ranking based on our estimates of these probabilities. Funny thing — it occurs that the Qini metric (which is often used for uplift measurement and will be described further) will assign better score to the imperfect ranking. How could it be?

Throughout this article, Qini and IPW are calibrated to match DR at one reference: the true-CATE ranking in the higher-selectivity, seed-42 holdout. The constants stay fixed for all learners, bootstrap resamples, assignment policies and tuning results. This aligns the reference scores, but does not adjust for confounding or change the ordering of models within a metric. In this example, calibrated Qini still favors Linear DR over the true-CATE ranking, whereas known causal gain favors true CATE. The calibration formula is given below.

The reason is that it’s often not enough to use a causal model that accounts for the confounding. If we have the treatment assignment dependent on the customer characteristics, we also need to adjust the metric to evaluate this causal model, as the Qini metric still can contain the selection bias.

In this article, we will go through the whole evolution of our attempts to measure the causal effect — from the uplift bars, through the Qini metric towards the IPW and doubly robust scores to evaluate the models. We will use six common learners from S learner to DML learner, and will see how we can assess their estimates depending on different degrees of confounding.

For a given treatment T (a marketing message) and an outcome Y (a customer’s actual purchase) a customer’s Conditional Average

CATE can be perceived as the average treatment effect (ATE) for a given customer with profile x. It can be used for customer targeting since high CATE shows that the the effect of the treatment on this customer is higher. Just to highlight — it doesn’t mean the customer with high CATE has the highest outcome or the probability of making some action. It means that if contacted, the customer has the highest uplift in this outcome or probability compared to the situation when the customer isn’t contacted.

Usually, companies have limited budgets for their marketing activities, so the ranking is instrumental to understand how to optimally distribute the budget for these activities.

In this article, we will compare the 6 models based on the synthetic data using different metrics. In our case we know the true treatment effect, which is usually not the case. This approach allows us to make a comparison and study the uplift metrics in detail.

It represents the difference in treatment probability, depending on the user profile. Irrespective of the metric and evaluation method and the model — we need some number of conditions to be satisfied so that our causal estimator works: consistency, no relevant interference, no unmeasured confounding and overlap.

We simulate 1 million individual synthetic customers for which we have several characteristics: age, income, past spending over time, time since last contact with the customer. We simulate a factual communication policy that depends on the two dimensions: age and last contact activity,

where a is the intercept for calibration, and Z is the standardized product of age and last contact activity. We have provided the executable code for the outcome in the companion.

To simulate this type of data, the following parameters are fixed for the communication policy: the probability is to be between 0.1 and 0.9, with 50% treated on average. The inactivity and age of the customer are used to predict the probability of communication with the customer.

The purchase probability is also based on a logistic function and dependent on customer characteristics. Moreover, the treatment effect itself is nonuniform and impacts different customers in a different way.

Below in the code you may see the simulation algorithm:

For every profile we calculate p₁(x), p₀(x) and TrueCATE=p₁(x)−p₀(x). As the treatment groups in the simulation are almost of equal size the mean of the true-CATE values for the treated customers is approximately +0.191 and for the controls −0.003. The observed purchase-rate difference is 0.119. The ATE for this simulation is 0.094 (all numbers are rounded to 3 FP digits).

Below are the graphs which allow us to have a high-level understanding of the data we have generated:

We trained on 700k customers and then evaluated on the 300k held-out customers using seed 42 for this example. Each of the S, T, X, DA, DR, DML estimators was implemented using both linear and “boosted” base models. Note that all of the estimators above (S,T,X,DA,DR,DML) have lengthy derivations and are material for another article. Here I will just provide the high-level intuition of the algorithms.

The models used for this article are the EconML implementations (the S- and T-learners as well as the DA-, DR-, and DML-learners with a linear and XGBoost base model).

Our starting point will be an S-learner as the simplest and the most intuitive model. Its holdout MSE against the true CATE is 0.0006, with correlation 0.9964. That tells us its effect estimates are quite accurate in this simulation. But in reality we don’t know the true effect, so we need another way to assess targeting.

The most obvious way to do this is an uplift barplot. We sort customers by the CATE, divide them into buckets and compare treatment and control outcomes for the buckets.

The graphs look useful: the right-hand buckets have larger observed differences than the left-hand ones. However, those differences are not quite the true effects. Grouping by predicted CATE does not necessarily make the treatment and control customers comparable inside each bucket — they can be very different in their characteristics.

The plot helps us inspect a model, but we should not interpret its bar differences as causal effects or use only them to decide who should receive treatment.

Quite often we just need one number, which allows us to compare different estimators. Something similar to the ROC AUC score we sometimes use to assess classification models. That’s where the Qini AUC comes into play.

Instead of having a bar plot that compares uplift for a number of different buckets of customers, look at the single customer with the highest predicted value of treatment. Then add the next customer with the highest predicted value, then the next customer, and so on. For each customer added in the group we calculate the total positive outcomes for the treatment and control.

Rₜ(k) and R꜀(k) denote the positive-outcome totals for the treatment group and the control group, respectively, for the top k customers. Let Nₜ (k) and N꜀ (k) denote the arm sizes for the treatment group and the control group.

Let p̂=Nₜ(N)/N be the observed treatment share in the evaluation sample. First, define q(f)=Q(k)/(Np̂), where f=k/N, and let A_Q be its area above the line connecting the start and end points:

Zero is the reference area for random targeting; finite-sample scores can fluctuate around it. The normalization by N and horizontal fraction f=k/N are already included above, so we do not divide this area by N² again. Dividing by the treatment share supplies the causal-gain unit convention, but does not remove selection bias.

For the additional calibration, let r₀ denote the true-CATE ranking in the higher-selectivity, seed-42 holdout. We use DR as the reference score and calculate the fixed divisors:

All displayed evaluation areas and differences then use:

All three reference scores are therefore start as 0.0826. The curve below is also divided by c_Q, so its area matches the tables. This is an oracle-assisted calibration for this simulation: it requires knowing the true-CATE ranking and does not establish that the scores estimate the same quantity accurately. They are calibrated only for comparability purposes. The calibration preserves each evaluator’s model ordering. We freeze these constants everywhere, including within bootstrap resamples.

Numbers are rounded for display. Differences and confidence intervals are calculated before rounding, so equal displayed scores need not be identical.

Here is the S-learner’s Qini curve for the illustration:

The main problem is that the Qini metric in its evaluation still uses the observed treatments and outcome variables. Remember that the customers were selected for treatment based on their characteristics; thus, the treatment/control differences still contain selection bias.

A causal learner estimates the treatment effect. If done correctly, it is potentially unconfounded. But the metric is still confounded, as it is observational! We’ve seen it already at the graph with the uplift bars — the difference was not matching the true effect.

This mismatch might be an insignificant calculation artifact if it wasn’t for its potential effect on qualitative conclusions based on the analysis. In our example, when we compare the models, the Linear DR learner gives us better metrics than the “oracle” model, which knows the true CATE. This is indicative of a large problem. Now we know we can’t trust Qini, because it can choose a wrong estimator for us.

Therefore, we now understand that we need to improve not just a learner, but the evaluation as well. The ideal situation of course — randomized treatment assignment. But when we have only biased observational data — we can use Inverse-Propensity Weighting (IPW) or Doubly Robust (DR) score which we discuss below.

Inverse-propensity weighting gives each observed outcome a weight based on how likely its assignment was:

Doubly robust scoring also uses the outcome prediction and the residual, but weights the residual by the inverse propensity score of the customer.

In the formulas above, T means the treatment flag, Y — the outcome variable. ê(X_i) — the propensity model (probability of being treated), μ̂₀(X_i) and μ̂₁(X_i) — the models of the outome prediction under treatment and control.

Usually, the DR-learner uses the same pseudo-outcome as you see above to fit effects, but here we are not looking for it — we are evaluating a trained ranking. The ranking can come from any model — not just the DR-learner.

Next step — we sort customers by the model-ranked scores, summing up the corresponding scores:

These are the uncalibrated IPW and DR gain curves. IPW and DR adjust for confounding under their respective assumptions. Under randomized assignment, treatment-share-normalized Qini targets the same causal-gain convention. For display throughout this article, we additionally divide the IPW curve and area by the fixed reference divisor c_IPW; DR stays unchanged. Calibration is separate from the causal adjustment.

For the adjusted methods, we estimate a propensity model and two outcome models separately from the main ranking model. They are called the nuisance models. They are estimated using the observable variables X, T, and Y. For the nuisance models, we use three-fold crossfitting, which guarantees that for both predictions the customer was excluded from the training sample for the models. All rankings use the same evaluation scores.

Running the following Python code in the companion directory trains the S-learner and, in addition, fits separate evaluation models.

The errors in the evaluation of different estimators are close to each other, so we better look at the error of the score of each ranking with respect to the causal gain of that ranking, which is known from the data generation process (thanks to our synthetic dataset!).

After calibration, Qini’s residual errors across the six boosted rankings range from +0.0002 to +0.0008. Calibrated IPW errors range from +0.0001 to +0.0002, and DR errors from +0.0001 to +0.0002. Qini favors the wrong ranking in the Linear-DR comparison below.

The disagreement matters for model choice, too:

The “true gain” is the area above the endpoint diagonal of the cumulative true-CATE curve for each ranking. IPW and DR produce scores close to these known gains and favor the true-CATE ranking over Linear DR. They do not reproduce every small ordering difference among the boosted learners. Calibrated Qini still favors Linear DR over the true-CATE ranking.

When you use these methods — keep in mind that IPW still requires a correct propensity model, and DR still requires a correct propensity OR both outcome models. Both scorers require consistency, no unmeasured confounding and overlap. Estimated models and finite samples leave residual error, so these approaches are not automatically unbiased scores for every dataset. So, you use it, but be careful as always.

We have only compared point estimates for the different models so far. It might be interesting to see how large the differences are between the estimates for another random set of evaluation customers (i.e. different realization of the holdout sample of 300k customers with their respective multiplicities). In other words — are these differences statistically significant and consistent?

In order to investigate this we conducted 1,000 paired bootstrap resamples of the 300,000 customers in the holdout data set. For each of the resampled evaluation data sets, we computed the statistics of interest for all models and all evaluation methods. The resulting values’ 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles are provided in brackets below.

These are the conditional 95% percentile intervals. Note that we hold the trained models and nuisance functions fixed and resampling only the evaluation part. This means we don’t guarantee the 95% coverage for the full procedure bootstrap. The experiment is repeated later with 3 different seeds to ensure the conclusions are robust.

Note that overlying intervals do not directly answer questions of whether one model is better than another. More relevant are the intervals for the paired differences between the two models under consideration (how much one model is better than another). Below we compared each of the models with the oracle truth.

Choosing a CATE estimator is a broader topic that deserves a separate article. For this example, I would choose the XGBoost S-learner as a simple starting point. It has the simplest estimation structure among the six learners considered: one outcome model, with treatment included as an input feature. The DML estimator has the highest DR-gain point estimate among the six boosted learners, but its advantage over S is small: the paired S-minus-DML difference is -0.00006, with a conditional 95% interval which includes zero. That does not prove equivalence and this is not the claim that S learner is always the best. But if the difference in the 5th digit is not critical for your application, I would choose the S-learner for this specific case. Simplicity wins.

The comparison of S with T has a positive DR-area difference of +0.0002 with a Conditional 95% Interval of [+0.00003, +0.0003]. So, within these models and this fixed set of nuisance fits, S has a statistically significant DR-area difference compared with T. The paired intervals for the comparisons with X, DA, DR, and DML all include zero, so there is no evidence of a consistently higher DR area for S.

We don’t use Qini here anymore, because we’ve seen before that its confoundedness affects its conclusions even on a qualitative scale. Even increasing bootstrap sample for the Qini won’t make it unbiased, so we can stop using it.

We have so far followed one data generation to model comparison example. Let’s now slightly change the assignment policy and check if the results are stable under different assignments.

We will replace 2.5 in the propensity rule by 0.5 and by 1, affecting the selection bias and we will call it “low” and “middle” selectivity. The population treatment share will still be 50% as we have calibrated our assignment in this way. We will also refit all the learners for 3 different seeds for robustness.

For this figure, we rank customers directly by their known true CATE. No S, T or other learner supplies the ranking. We hold the customer profiles and this perfect ordering fixed across assignment policies within each seed, then change which customers receive treatment and which outcomes we observe. The question is whether each evaluator can accurately score the same ranking as assignment becomes more selective.

All three evaluators’ point estimates will coincide in the “higher” selection policy by construction because of the calibration we’ve done for comparability. The valibration is made based on the true CATE and we are considering the true CATE ranking in this case. What is interesting is how the rankers behave in case of the changes in the assignment policy.

We see that the DR and IPW behave quite stable, and the Qini is not stable at all and changing a lot depending on the assignment policy. This is one more evidence of how it can be influenced by different levels of selection bias.

All three runs of increased selectivity show the same reversal between Linear DR and true CATE as was seen in the single run of increased selectivity. The expected-count diagnostic is also well-behaved. This constitutes more empirical evidence for the phenomenon than a single lucky or unlucky run. (Of course, three runs do not guarantee to cover the variability in all possible datasets.)

What about hyperparameter tuning? The evaluator also affects which hyperparameters do we select! We gave each of the six boosted learners 15 configurations, including its default. The original 700,000 training customers were split into 500,000 for fitting candidates and 200,000 for validation. Then we selected each learner’s configuration using cross-fitted DR gain on that validation sample, without using true CATE.

Then we have frozen the selected hyperparameters before generating a fresh 300,000-customer test sample from the ”high” selectivity policy. Both default and selected models were refitted on the same original 700,000 training customers, then evaluated on these new test customers with shared cross-fitted evaluation models. The earlier article holdout was not used in this tuning comparison. So, do not attribute differences from earlier tables to tuning alone. Below you will see the illustrated effect of the tuning on the three metrics considered before and on the RMSE metric which is calculated relative to the true CATE which we know as we have generated our dataset (it’s omitted from other sections, because in reality we never know the true CATE).

The direction of the effect from our tuning is not clear for S, X, DA, DR, DML learners as the intervals include zero, which corresponds to no change in the values. But for T-learner the paired intervals all favor tuning which also improves the CATE RMSE from 0.0328 to 0.0237. S-learner has the most extreme behavior where the DR point estimate decreased, and the CATE RMSE increased from 0.0243 to 0.0316 on the fresh test sample. So our tuning in case of the S-learner was not very fruitful.

To be clear, it’s still hard to compare the tuning of such different models, as the number of potential hyperparameter changes is different for a simple S-learner and for the DML. But the idea of this section is to show that the hyperparameter runing doesn’t change the ranking effect of confounded metric (Qini) we’ve shown before.

In conclusion, let’s try to formulate — what should we do when comparing the uplift models quality? First evaluate the assignment to treatment in your experiment. If the assignment to treatment is not random (as in most cases) then a familiar uplift plot or Qini curve don’t work anymore. Use both an evaluation design and the estimator which assumptions still hold (don’t require random assignment).

Using IPW and a DR evaluator of causal gain on the the data gave scores close to the known causal gain and kept the estimators ranking correct. I would opt in for the DR evaluation, well, because it’s Doubly Robust, so it’s still valid even if one of its assumptions failed.

Ultimately, for your marketing campaign (or any other application of the uplift model) look at what’s important for your case: the budget, cost and incremental value for a given budget. Area under the curve is interesting but not what you ar optimizing for as the business objective.

The separate evaluation companion contains evaluation.ipynb, the shared model and metric implementation, all numerical tables, paired bootstrap draws, figures and the tuning protocol. Its default notebook run analyzes the completed experiments and independently checks IPW/DR formulas from stored observed rows and nuisance predictions.

python reproduce.py --output regenerated recreates all baseline fits, evaluator fits, diagnostics, resamples, tuning and figures in a new directory. The single code example above is supplied as article_example.py. The README distinguishes these full fitting steps from quick notebook analysis. Three-policy seed ranges and fixed-fit bootstrap intervals retain their separate meanings.

[1] PyWhy, EconML Meta-Learners, version 0.16.0 documentation.

[2] E. H. Kennedy, Towards optimal doubly robust estimation of heterogeneous causal effects (2020; revised 2023), arXiv.

[3] scikit-uplift contributors, Metric implementation, version 0.5.1 documentation.

[4] grf contributors, Assessing heterogeneity with RATE, documentation. Our own conditional row-bootstrap procedure is used in this article instead of grf’s implementation of RATE for causal heterogeneity inference.

Staff Data Scientist at Careem. Writing about causal inference, experimentation, and practical AI—from model assumptions to real decisions.

#9771. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Email Marketing


1. Why is email marketing important?

Email is the marketing tool that helps you  create a seamless, connected, frictionless buyer journey. More importantly, email marketing allows you to build relationships with prospects, customers, and past customers. It's your chance to speak  to them right in their inbox, at a time that suits them. Along with the right message, email can become one of your most powerful marketing channels.

2. What is benefits of email marketing?

Email marketing is best way for creating long term relationship with your clients, and increasing sales in our company.

Benefits of email marketing for bussiness:
  • Better brand recognition
  • Statistics of what works best
  • More sales
  • Targeted audience
  • More traffic to your products/services/newsletter
  • Build credibility
Most  bussinesses are using email marketing and making tons of money with email marketing.

3. What is the simplest day and time to send my marketing emails?


Again, the answer to this question varies from company to company. And again, testing is the way to find out what works best. Typically, weekends and mornings seem to be  times when multiple emails are opened, but since your audience may have different habits, it's best to experiment and then use your  data to decide.

 4. Which metrics should I be looking at?


The two most important metrics for email marketing are  open rate and click-through rate. If your emails aren't opened, subscribers will never see your full marketing message, and if they open them but don't click through to your site, your emails won't convert.

5. How do I write a decent subject line?


The best subject lines are short and to the point, accurately describing  the content of the email, but also catchy and intriguing, so the reader wants to know more. Once Again, this is the perfect place for  A/B testing, to see what types of subject lines work best with your audience. Your call to action should be clear and  simple. It should be somewhere at the top of your email for those who haven't finished reading the entire email,  then repeated  at the end for those reading all the way through. It should state exactly what you want subscribers to do, for example "Click here to download the premium theme for free.




6. Is email marketing still effective?

Email marketing is one of the most effective ways for a business to reach its customers directly. Think about it. You don't post something on your site  hoping people will visit it. You don't even post something on a social media page and hope fans  see it. You're sending something straight to each person's inbox, where they'll definitely  see it! Even if they don't open it, they'll still see your subject line and business name every time you send an email, so you're still communicating directly with your audience.



7. However do I grow my email subscribers list? Should i buy an email list or build it myself?

Buying an email list is  waste of time & money. These email accounts are unverified and not interested in your brand. The mailing list is useless if your subscribers do not open your emails. There are different ways to grow your mailing list. 

Give them a free ebook and host it on a landing page where they have to enter the email to download the file and also create a forum page on your website, asks your visitors what questions they might have about your business, and collects email addresses to follow up with them.


8. How do I prevent audience from unsubscribing?


If the  subject line of the email is irrelevant to  customers, they will ignore it multiple times. But, if it keeps repeating, they are intercepted and unsubscribed from your emails. So, send relevant emails for the benefit of the customer. Don't send emails that often only focus  on sales, offers and discounts. 
Submit information about your business and offers so you can connect with customers. You can also update them on recent trends in your industry. The basic role of an email is first and foremost to  connect with customers, get the most out of this tool.

9. What is the difference between a cold email and a spam email?


Cold emails are mostly sales emails that are sent with content align to the needs of the recipient. It is usually personalized and includes a business perspective. However, it is still an unsolicited email. And all unsolicited emails are marked as SPAM. 
Regularly receiving this type of unsolicited email in your users' inboxes, chances are  your emails will soon be diverted to  spam or junk folders. The most important thing to prevent this from happening is to respect your recipients' choice to opt-out of receiving emails from you. You can add the links to easily unsubscribe. You must be familiar with the CAN-SPAM Act and its regulations.

10. Where can I find email template?

Almost all email campaign tools provide you with ready-made templates. Whether you use MailChimp or Pardot, you'll get several email templates ready to use.
 However, if you want to create a template from scratch, you can do so.Most of email campaign tools have option to paste the HTML code of your own design. 


11. What email marketing trend will help marketers succeed in 2022?

Is it a trend to listen to  and get to know your customers? I think people realize how bad it feels for a brand or a company to obsess over themselves without knowing their customers personal needs. People who listen empathetically and then provide value based on what they learn will win.


Final Saying


 You can approach email marketing in different ways. We have compiled a list of most frequently asked questions to help you understand how to get started, what constraints you need to keep in mind, and what future development you will need, we don’t have 100% answers to every situation and there’s always a chance you will have something new and different to deal with as you market your own business.

#9770. LLMON: An LLM-Native Markup Language, now in Granite 4.1 3B and 8B

LLMs rely on their context to generate the next set of tokens. Over a long trajectory, the context fills with numerous types of components: a system prompt, past conversation turns, instructions that act on retrieved documents, tool responses or user data, requirements constraining the allowed output, and reasoning chains. The context carries a rich structure, most of which is either implicit to the model or encoded in formats such as JSON that were not designed to be digested by LLMs. This is one of the main reasons LLMs, particularly those on the smaller end of the scale, are brittle and sometimes fail in unexpected ways. The lack of explicit structure can also be exploited by attackers, for example, in the form of prompt injections.

To address this, we developed LLMON (LLM Object Notation, pronounced “lemon”), an LLM-native markup language for explicitly communicating structure and semantics to the models. Semantically coherent components are marked with meaningful tags which are wrapped in reserved special-token delimiters. Data schemas, including nesting, are stated in a way that is unambiguous to a causal LLM. Unique IDs make it possible to point to specific instructions, which could reside anywhere in the context, and bind them to the data payloads they should act on, analogous to the way functions are called and arguments are passed to them in programming languages.

Today we are releasing two experimental preview models, derived from Granite 4.1 base models, trained to consume and generate LLMON-marked text: granite-4.1-3b-LLMON-preview and granite-4.1-8b-LLMON-preview. We are also releasing a GitHub repo, which includes a toolkit for working with LLMON and examples of workflows and templates.

JSON was designed for parsers, not for causal language models. The tokenizer is not constrained to respect the grammar, and structure is encoded by tokens ({, ", :) that may also appear in normal text. To a model, a quotation mark inside a document and a quotation mark that closes a field are the same token. Escaping rules that are clear to a parser are only statistical patterns to a model. Nesting depth is encoded by counting brackets, which transformers are known to be weak at, especially over long spans.

LLMON, on the other hand, is an XML-like markup whose structural delimiters are reserved special tokens rather than characters, so structure and content use separate parts of the vocabulary. Tags are stated at the beginning of each span, and the boundaries between spans are explicit. Nested structures are stated locally so the model does not need to keep track of the hierarchy over long spans.

Since most teams already have pipelines built around JSON, we created conversion tools and example notebooks that translate JSON to LLMON and back in a lossless manner.

LLMON does not replace chat templates; rather, it enriches them. Where regular chat templates tell the model which part belongs to which role (system, user, assistant), LLMON tells it what each component means and how components relate to each other, within and across roles.

The LLMON preview models ship with their own chat template, so you build the same messages list you would pass to any chat model and call apply_chat_template as usual; it renders the LLMON shown below. The only difference is that a turn can now name its parts and mark each one exec: True or False. A part marked True is bound into the exec block at the bottom of the rendered output, which states which instruction to run and what it operates on; a part marked False is still rendered into the context but is referenced by nothing.

Which the model receives as the following (with newlines and indentation added here for readability, as the template emits none):

The two-character block IDs are drawn from a fixed set that this tokenizer encodes as single tokens, so addressing a block always costs two tokens regardless of which ID is drawn.

The role is still a single user turn, but its components reach the model as five separate addressable blocks, bound together by a sixth (the exec block) that states: run this instruction, on this data, subject to these two requirements, and put the answer in the block named here, which is the same assistant block the model then fills. A conventional template would have flattened all components into one string and left the model to infer which part was the task, which was the subject, and which were constraints.

Indirect prompt injection is a type of attack where a malicious instruction is hidden in a data payload, such as a retrieved document, a tool response, or user-provided data. This is the problem LLMON’s instruction/data separation is designed to address.

We compared the LLMON previews against several open-source and closed-source models. We evaluated on the OPI benchmark, which places the injection in the data of classic NLP tasks. Several attack strategies are employed. We report robustness, defined as 1 − attack success rate: the share of attacks where the model does not carry out the injected instruction.

All non-LLMON models are highly susceptible, carrying out the injected instructions with high probability. LLMON practically eliminates the problem on this benchmark, avoiding 47% more attacks relative to the best frontier model that we tested, and 95% more than the best open-source model. We observe similar trends on other benchmarks (ASB and StruQ). It is worth noting that these benchmarks test robustness to static indirect prompt injections. The instruction/data separation directly addresses this type of attack. We are actively working on also improving adaptive attacks which unfold over many chat turns.

Safety gains don’t come at the expense of general capability. Across standard benchmark categories, the LLMON models perform on par with the Granite 4.1 Instruct models.

In short, if you’re experimenting with Granite 4.1 3B or 8B today, you can swap in the LLMON preview and should see comparable general performance with much stronger resistance to prompt injection. No conversion pipeline is required. Naming the turn's parts (e.g., instruction, data, requirement as in the example above) is enough. The shipped chat template turns those into LLMON blocks for you. Our LLMON-converters library goes one level deeper: if a part is itself structured, such as a JSON document, LLMONizing it preserves that structure as typed, individually addressable blocks, instead of one opaque string.

The models start from Granite 4.1 base checkpoints rather than the released instruct models, so LLMON behavior is learned during post-training rather than layered on an existing chat format.

LLMON defines six delimiters that mark the start and end of tags and allow nesting and anchoring; they are installed in the tokenizer as reserved single tokens. We re-serialized a conventional instruction-tuning corpus into LLMON: every prompt component becomes its own addressable block, and each turn carries an execution block naming which instruction to run, which inputs it operates on, and where the output goes. The task mix is the one a normal instruct model sees (chat, multi-turn, RAG, tool calling), which is why benchmark performance stays close to the conventionally tuned model. In addition, we augment the data with decoy instructions and data blocks that are present in context but deliberately left unbound, while the target output is unchanged. So the model learns to follow the dependencies dictated by the execution block and ignore the rest. Reinforcement learning follows: five sequential GRPO stages spanning multi-domain reasoning, RLHF, knowledge calibration, and math, followed by a final DPO stage on a thousand on-policy preference pairs built from the model’s own responses to injection attempts.

The resulting privilege rule falls out of this layout rather than an added guardrail: an instruction reached through an execution block is authoritative, while anything reached as input (data, documents, tool schemas, tool results) is material to read, not a command to follow. Furthermore, instructions and data spans that are not called on in the execution block are ignored. This is a learned behavior, not an enforced guarantee. To see how this plays out in the attention layers of a LLMON model, try the LLMON Attention Visualization on Hugging Face Spaces.

LLMON is not tied to a fixed schema: you can choose tag names and structure that fit your domain and fine-tune an adapter to read and write them. We demonstrate this on ScienceWorld, a text-based benchmark where an agent carries out elementary science tasks (such as boiling water) by issuing one command at a time and receiving a score from the simulator. We defined a vocabulary capturing the structure in the planning trajectories involved in solving these tasks. The vocabulary includes tags such as instr.task.goal, req.planning_policy.rule, data.state.room, data.state.inventory and assistant.next_action. We rendered every step of ScienceWorld's reference solutions with these tags and tuned a LoRA on top of a LLMON model. The trained model then plays held-out games and writes its next action in the new vocabulary. This notebook walks through the full workflow, from converting reference trajectories to playing the test games and scoring the adapter against the untrained base model. Another example for tool-calling agents can be found in this notebook.

This is an experimental preview, ready for exploration and evaluation but not for production.

Tell us what you find: what worked, what broke, and which use cases you’d like to see. Post it in GitHub Discussions.

This is an interesting development, especially the idea of giving LLMs a more explicit structure for understanding instructions, data, and their relationships. The discussion about prompt injection and separating instructions from input data is particularly relevant as organizations build more advanced LLM applications. Implementing these approaches requires engineers who understand model behavior, fine-tuning, context management, and evaluation. #9769. Want to Rent an Internet Address at the White House?

Several staffers at the White House are using computers or mobile devices equipped with residential proxy services that render their internet address available for others to rent, security experts warned today. One of the proxy services is a Russian company whose founder’s web hosting business was ground zero for cyberattacks against election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

The security firm Layer3 Intel said it detected multiple residential proxy nodes beaconing out from the internet address network reserved for the Executive Office of the President (AS2650). Layer3 said the proxy activity was relatively persistent between October 5 to November 3, and that a review of the proxies available from AS2650 showed they exited from the White House network 236 times during that period.

The proxy tracking company Synthient said on Twitter/X that the activity it saw coming from AS2650 was related to multiple Windows 11 installations of a service called Infatica, a proxy program that is often integrated into “free” mobile and desktop applications. Infatica’s founder Vladimir Fomenko is a Russian man whose hosting firm King Servers was home to six of the eight internet addresses used by Russia’s state security services to compromise databases for election systems in Arizona and Illinois in 2016.

Synthient’s depiction of the outgoing proxy traffic from the dedicated White House network (AS2650). Click to enlarge.

There are dozens of residential proxy providers with varying degrees of legitimacy, many of them based in China or Russia. But at a minimum, they all make it simple for customers to rent someone else’s internet address as a way to anonymize their web traffic or spoof their true location. From a website’s perspective, the traffic from a proxy network user appears to originate from the rented IP address, not from the proxy service customer.

Layer3 Intel said the proxy exit nodes at the White House came from six internet addresses, on 26 of the 30 days, and that most of the activity happens in the evening, between 5 p.m. and midnight.

Incredibly, Infatica was not the only proxy service that reportedly has been reselling access to White House internet addresses: Layer3 Intel said it found 28 separate residential proxy services were able to exit through this network.

“This is public access,” the Layer3 Intel team wrote. “Anybody can obtain it by signing up to a public residential proxy service, paying a few dollars and sending requests through it. We did not selectively target this network or try to make our probes exit from it. We caught this by chance, simply by requesting global rotating access through these services.”

The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

As detailed in several stories here over the past year, residential proxy services are a major source of unwanted and often malicious traffic, including account takeover and other cybercrime activity, advertising fraud, and mass content scraping for AI projects.

They can also introduce serious security risks. In late 2025, it was discovered that cybercriminals were mass exploiting a widespread vulnerability in these services that allowed them to probe each proxy endpoint’s local network for vulnerable systems to infect with malware. In January 2026, dozens of proxy services were forced to patch their networks after Synthient Founder Ben Brundage showed how cybercriminals were abusing a vulnerability in these residential proxy services to seize control over devices inside the local networks of unsuspecting users.

“Some of these resellers sell bandwidth for as low as 60 cents a Gigabyte, that means for less than a dollar you can gain access into some of the most confidential and trusted networks,” Brundage told KrebsOnSecurity. “The reseller ecosystem further enables this with any criminal able to buy access while skipping KYC [Know Your Customer] processes.”

All too often, these proxy services are beaconing out from employee devices brought into the workplace. App developers can embed software development kits (SDKs) provided by the residential proxy networks to monetize their software, allowing them to receive a small amount of money on each installation.

As risky as residential proxies can be for unsuspecting end users, they are all too commonly found on government and corporate networks. In a webinar in January 2026, the proxy tracking service Spur found residential proxies in nearly 300 government owned and operated networks, 318 utility companies, 166 healthcare companies or hospitals, and 141 companies in banking and finance. In a blog post earlier this year, the security firm Infoblox said it discovered that fully 65% of its customer base was querying one or more residential proxy related domains.

The idea of leasing out address space tied to a government block is fascinating, but the real worry is how much trust downstream networks place in who announces a prefix. If BGP origin validation is not airtight, a rented slice with a White House label is a gift to anyone doing phishing or traffic hijacks.

What struck me is how mundane the mechanism is: a staffer installs a free app, and suddenly a government IP becomes rentable inventory. Egress filtering and device policy on staff phones seem like a far cheaper fix than anything fancy at the routing layer.

One useful technical distinction is that AS2650 is an autonomous system, not a single subnet. For an observed exit IP, investigators still need the timestamp, the then-current BGP origin and prefix, RDAP allocation data, and corroborating telemetry; registration or geolocation alone does not identify the device or the proxy customer. That matters when a residential proxy makes traffic look trusted simply because the address falls inside an organization’s announced space. I maintain OnlinTools; our Subnet Calculator can show the network, range, broadcast address and host count for a supplied CIDR prefix, but it cannot establish route origin, physical location, ownership, or compromise.

Interesting how a seemingly ordinary device can turn a trusted network into an access point for someone else’s traffic.

What makes this particularly concerning is that the organization may remain completely unaware of how its own infrastructure is being used. A good reminder that information security also depends on visibility into what is actually happening within a network.

The location detail is what separates this from ordinary proxy noise: AS2650 is a fixed, well-known allocation, so any exit node registered there is either a misconfiguration worth escalating internally or an actual beacon worth watching – there’s no third reading. That Infatica nodes bundled into free apps are the vector fits the broader pattern where the resource being rented out belongs to someone who never knowingly agreed to rent it. The persistent two-week window suggests nobody at the network’s edge was watching egress, which is the cheap fix here.

#9768. Critical PHP Flaws Allow Code Execution, but Don't Panic 'PHP2Shell'-Style

November's monthly security release patches seven critical PHP flaws that should be addressed ASAP, though experts say exploitability varies and depends heavily on configuration.

The PHP team has released a new security update that fixes a wide swath of vulnerabilities and issues, but compared with last month's PHP2Shell chaos, it's harder to pin down how much these bugs will appeal to attackers.

That's because, according to PHP's maintainers, the seven issues rated "critical" in the latest monthly security update "require either non-default configuration or uncommon setups." The update, published Nov. 19, affects all supported versions of PHP, and maintainers strongly encourage users to upgrade promptly.

This latest update comes on the heels of threat actors targeting PHP2Shell — a pair of vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) capable of remote code execution (RCE) in PHP — en masse. PHP is an open source scripting language common in Web development and present in much of the server infrastructure keeping the Internet afloat. Given PHP's ubiquity, the rush to patch created a fervor across the security industry hardly seen since Log4Shell in 2021.

Related:Cursor Traces Malicious Claude Code Extensions to Third-Party Breach

PHP versions 8.2 through 8.5 now have patches available through the project's downloads page, in the form of 8.2.36, 8.3.37, 8.4.28, and 8.5.13. 8.6.0; the latest major release of PHP also launched today with fixes included.

Of the dozens of issues accounted for in the changelog, the seven marked critical (CVSS 9.2) on GitHub were: session serializer mismatch RCE flaw CVE-2026-115560; use-after-free via repopulation of last_fatal_error_backtrace global after shutdown flaw CVE-2026-129182; time zone cache use-after-free RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-129496; use-after-free after interrupted session shutdown bug CVE-2026-129481; use-after-free in magic method backtraces RCE bug CVE-2026-129474; PHP-FPM request smuggling through an unread HTTP request body bug CVE-2026-129289; and PHP file-based session handler RCE vulnerability CVE-2026-126714.

While maintainers included workarounds in most critical advisories (barring CVE-2026-115560), they're considered temporary mitigations, and users should upgrade as soon as they can.

Justin Moore, director of adversary operations at Arctic Wolf, tells Dark Reading that two challenges organizations will run into when patching these issues are business continuity for servers running critical functions and visibility.

"A lot of organizations don’t have a complete inventory of where PHP is running, especially with legacy applications, internally developed Web services, managed hosting environments, or third-party software. It's baked into CMS platforms, hosting control panels, vendor appliances, and old internal apps," he says. "When a vulnerability is disclosed, the primary challenge is identifying every aspect of the business that is affected. The reality is that Internet-facing PHP systems should move toward the front of the patch queue because attackers have repeatedly demonstrated an interest in rapidly exploiting PHP vulnerabilities when a path to code execution exists."

Related:Grok Bots Attempt to Access Corporate Data Without User Approval

Among the critical flaws, there are some that experts recommend focusing on first. According to Upwind, which published an analysis of the security release, PHP-FPM bug CVE-2026-129289 is the one to close first, because it "gives an unauthenticated attacker PHP code execution with a single request," with no memory corruption, gadget chain, or race required to exploit. Although Upwind assesses it's the most direct route to code execution, "It does need a front end that reuses FastCGI connections and an application path that opens php://input without reading it to the end."

Upwind also noted that three of the vulnerabilities address gaps introduced by the PHP2Shell fixes last month. "PHP ties CVE-2026-129481 and CVE-2026-129182 to cases the October fix for CVE-2026-109619 did not cover," according to the analysis. "A third, CVE-2026-129474, became remotely reachable through a change introduced in 8.5.12."

Related:F-Secure Identifies 26 Ways AI Can Harm Consumers, and Where to Stop Them

All three depend on specific configurations and versions. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 are only applicable to PHP 8.5, while CVE-2026-129481 excludes PHP 8.2. CVE-2026-129474 and CVE-2026-129182 both rely on PHP 8.5's fatal error backtrace engine feature, which was introduced with that version; for CVE-2026-129481, the session cleanup behavior it exploits was introduced in PHP 8.3.

Finally, among the other recommendations the analysis makes, one broader tip may ring true for a wide range of PHP-using organizations: "Don't forget container images and appliances that bundle their own PHP build. They need a rebuild or a vendor update."

Meanwhile, WatchTowr's Jake Knott tells Dark Reading that CVE-2026-115560, CVE-2026-126714, and CVE-2026-129289 are the ones the firm expects attackers to go after first.

In any case, while not the same level of emergency as seen last month, users should absolutely apply this latest update as soon as they can.

Just because a vulnerability is rated critical does not necessarily mean it applies to all organizations equally or that threat actors will target each issue like the PHP2Shell bugs last month.

Knott, who is WatchTowr's head of threat intelligence, says organizations must consider factors such as how a vulnerability is exploited and how likely real-world exploitation is. And more specifically, whether that organization uses the affected configurations or meets the prerequisites for exploitation. Only then can one determine where attackers have a viable path and how defenders can prioritize securing their environments.

He says the best place to start is with three questions. First, how is PHP being run (be it PHP-FPM, Apache mod_php, php-cgi, or something else)? Second, how are sessions configured, and is session upload progress enabled? And third, what settings is PHP running with, and where are errors being logged?

"Organizations should absolutely take these vulnerabilities seriously, and many of the other critical and high-rated vulnerabilities from this week," Knott says. "There is a stark difference in business-as-usual accelerated patching in response to a critical vulnerability, and panic driven by trivially exploitable default configuration vulnerabilities that typically carry the product2shell monikers, which these aren't."

He adds, "Answers to these questions will quickly rule out many of these vulnerabilities and let organizations patch prioritized sets of assets from a position of understanding and actual risk."

#9767. llama.cpp v1.0.0 : A stronger foundation for the local AI ecosystem

llama.cpp makes it possible to run multi-modal LLMs across a wide range of hardware - from consumer-grade local machines to high-end enterprise servers. Through quantization, optimized backends, and a portable C/C++ implementation, we make AI inference accessible at every level of the software stack. We believe this is the most lightweight, versatile and sensible platform for building cross-platform and private AI products.

Today we release libraries v1.0.0, highlighting our responsibility to those developers. Moving forward, both llama.cpp and ggml will reflect API and ABI incompatibilities with major-version bumps. As adoption grows, we will be stricter about making those boundaries visible to downstream consumers.

The following rules apply to all ggml-org projects using semantic versioning:

We are looking forward to expanding the ways in which ggml-org software is distributed and reaches developers and end-users. For more information about how to add ggml-org projects to your packaging and release pipelines, please check the following discussion.

The project has fostered an amazing open-source community with highly-skilled and talented contributors. With the rapid advance of AI capabilities in the field of software engineering, we continue to adapt and integrate LLMs in our developement cycle in a thoughtful and resonable manner. Maintaining a high quality codebase, staying in control of the architecture and understanding the implementation details will remain our top priorities.

To reinforce the faster pace of development we continue to invest more and more resources in improving the CI infrastructure behind the projects. Thanks to HF technologies such as HF Buckets and HF Jobs we are able to scale the capacity necessary to guarantee correctness for every change that lands on the master branches. With hardware support from NVIDIA, AMD, Qualcomm, Arm, IBM and Intel, we continue to enroll more self-hosted runners across all major hardware platforms.

The underlying machine learning engine of llama.cpp - ggml is designed to run on virtually any hardware in existence. This is achieved by implementing dedicated ggml backends. Each backend can be compiled as a dynamic library and optionally loaded at runtime.

A complete list of the currently implemented backends can be found here.

We are committed to provide continuous support of all model architectures. Currently, llama.cpp supports more than 150 architecture variants as well as all mainstream speculative decoding methods.

The llama.cpp team at Hugging Face is thankful for the incredible support from the community. Special thanks to the long-time maintainers of the project and all contributors. This is a significant milestone which would not have been possible without our joint efforts!
